Jack Gough, a representative of the Invasive Species Council, called Philip Island likely the best-prepared location in Australia, but noted that vaccination should have begun earlier. Todd emphasized that the detection of the virus in the little penguin is cause for concern, but experts advise continuing the vaccination program as quickly and safely as possible. Officials are also considering expanding the program to include vulnerable animal species in captivity.

World.title: Trump posts a map designating the Strait of Hormuz as "new US territory"
World.content:
Trump posts a map designating the Strait of Hormuz as “new US territory”

18th Tuesday, August 2026 - 22:06 UTC Full article

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday posted an image on his Truth Social platform showing a map of the Strait of Hormuz circled and captioned “NEW U.S. Territory,” above a band in the colours of the American flag. The post carried no accompanying text.

The circle drawn on the image also takes in a portion of mainland Iranian territory on the northern shore of the waterway, which separates the Persian Gulf from the Gulf of Oman. Before the conflict, around a fifth of the world's oil passed through the route.

Hours later, the president posted a second message: “There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect. The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated.”

On the same day, a merchant vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile in Omani waters of the strait as it was leaving the Persian Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency. Its engine room was damaged and the Omani coastguard was sent to rescue the crew. Commercial traffic remains far below levels seen before the conflict, which began on February 28.

Iran's deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, responded to the post on X. “The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech,” he wrote. “Iran neither fears threats nor cowers before displays of power.” Other Iranian officials dismissed the claim as nonsense.

Trump had trailed the idea on Friday at an event in Long Island, New York state. “After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” he said. “We have the blockade — no ships get through unless we want them to.” In the same speech he turned to Latin America: “And how about Venezuela? Venezuela was a one-day war, and now we work great with them. We've taken in millions and millions of barrels of oil.”

Since returning to the White House, the president has raised territorial claims over Greenland, the Panama Canal, Canada and Venezuela. Hormuz is a corridor of international waters bounded to the north by Iran and to the south by Oman. Claiming sovereignty over it contrasts with decades of declared US policy in favour of freedom of navigation, which Washington has defended through regular patrols in areas such as the South China Sea.

World.title: Petrobras confirms oil off the Amapá coast but cannot yet estimate the volume
World.content:
Petrobras confirms oil off the Amapá coast but cannot yet estimate the volume

18th Tuesday, August 2026 - 06:56 UTC Full article

Lula, who attended the event, highlighted the significance of the find for the country's future oil production but said it does not alter Brazil's strategy on renewable energy

Brazil's state-controlled Petrobras confirmed on Monday the presence of oil in the Morpho exploratory well, located in ultra-deep waters off the northern state of Amapá, in the Foz do Amazonas basin. The company cautioned that it cannot yet estimate the volume found or the viability of commercial production.

“There is oil, there is a discovery. We still do not know how much,” said the company's chief executive, Magda Chambriard, at an event in Oiapoque alongside President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The announcement confirms and refines one made last Friday, when Petrobras reported the identification of hydrocarbons in the well through wireline logs and rock indications.

Chambriard said around a thousand metres remain to be drilled to reach the bottom of the well and that the operation will be completed within 15 to 20 days. A delimitation phase will then begin, aimed at measuring the reservoir's extent and recoverable volume. A find in an exploratory well does not in itself amount to a commercially exploitable reserve.

The Morpho well lies some 175 kilometres off the Amapá coast and around 500 from the mouth of the Amazon, in a water depth of 2,886 metres. Petrobras operates block FZA-M-59 with a 100% stake, acquired in the eleventh bidding round of the National Petroleum Agency in 2013 under a concession regime. According to Chambriard, the company has invested some 3 billion dollars since the current exploratory campaign in the region began in August last year, at an operating cost of close to a million dollars a day.

Drilling in this basin was subject to a lengthy licensing process. The Brazilian Institute of the Environment initially rejected the request in 2023 and granted the permit in October 2025. Petrobras plans to drill three more wells in the same block and five in adjacent areas, subject to new environmental authorisations, and has already filed the corresponding applications.

Brazil's Equatorial Margin belongs to the same geological province as the fields developed in Guyana and Suriname, which explains industry interest in the area. Petrobras frames the exploration within its strategy of replenishing reserves.

Lula, who attended the event, highlighted the significance of the find for the country's future oil production but said it does not alter Brazil's strategy on renewable energy. “The country will continue to be the country of biofuel innovation and will continue to be very big on the question of renewable fuel,” he said. According to the president, Brazil will maintain investment in biofuels and other renewable sources while assessing the potential of new oil areas.

World.title: Argentina's vice-president says she is "extremely worried" about those who cannot make ends meet
World.content:
Argentina's vice-president says she is “extremely worried” about those who cannot make ends meet

18th Tuesday, August 2026 - 06:52 UTC Full article

“The political class has to start thinking about those issues, almost to the exclusion of everything else,” she added, speaking to farmers and reporters

Argentina's vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has again distanced herself from Javier Milei's government, voicing concern over unemployment and the financial difficulties facing households. “I am extremely worried about Argentines who today have no work or who cannot make ends meet,” she said at the opening of Expo Venado 2026, an agricultural fair in Venado Tuerto, Santa Fe province.

“The political class has to start thinking about those issues, almost to the exclusion of everything else,” she added, speaking to farmers and reporters. She argued that without work there is no family and without production there is no work, and that the country ought to have a successful future given its potential, though at present it “has many complexities.”

The remarks contrast with the executive's position on household debt. Arrears on credit to individuals reached 17.5% of total lending in June, according to a study by Universidad Austral and the consultancy Eco Go, and both Milei and his economy minister, Luis Caputo, have described the situation as a matter between private parties for the market to resolve.

Villarruel also called for the elimination of export duties, known in Argentina as retenciones, a levy applied for decades to overseas sales of grains and other products. She said farming and industry should operate without those taxes and argued that “the future of Argentina is agricultural and industrial.” She called for a policy of strong support for domestic industry.

The vice-president cut the ribbon alongside Leonel Chiarella, mayor of Venado Tuerto and president of the national committee of the Unión Cívica Radical, a party outside the governing coalition. Asked about the 2027 electoral landscape, she said it is “fundamental to think about national unity” without the debate being absorbed by discussion of “candidacies or political parties.”

Villarruel was Milei's running mate in the 2023 elections and presides over the Senate, but has maintained a distant relationship with the presidency for months. Figures close to the president have publicly called for her resignation.

That distance was visible again on Monday, when she was not invited to the official ceremony led by Milei marking the anniversary of the death of José de San Martín, the general who led the independence campaigns of Argentina, Chile and Peru and the central figure in the Argentine national pantheon. The vice-president marked the date on her X account, writing that “his example is the guide for Argentines who do not kneel and who defend national sovereignty every day.”

World.title: An infamous Morelos narco ranch will be converted into a school and health center
World.content:
A ranch in central Mexico formerly owned by convicted drug kingpin Edgar Valdez Villarreal — aka “La Barbie” — will be converted into a high school and health complex, Morelos Gov. Margarita González Saravia said Tuesday.

The property, known as El Paraíso, is in Atlacholoaya, roughly a 35-minute drive south of Cuernavaca, the Morelos state capital.

will house three entities: a technological agricultural high school; a center for traditional medicine; and an office of a 2-year-old state agency that promotes and supports Indigenous and Afro-Mexican communities.

The school, known by its Spanish initials CBTA, is intended to address a longstanding demand for secondary education infrastructure in the area. Its curriculum will be tied to traditional medicine and ancestral knowledge held by Morelos’ Indigenous communities.

Construction and renovation work is expected to begin in the coming weeks.

Authorities seized the property after Valdez’s former associate Arturo Beltrán Leyva was killed by Mexican Navy personnel in a 2009 raid of a Cuernavaca apartment complex.

The leader of the Beltrán Leyva organization at the time, Beltrán and his brothers had been senior figures in the Sinaloa Cartel before breaking away.

The ranch was later transferred to Indep, the federal agency that administers and disposes of assets seized by the government.

The National Lottery offered El Paraíso as one of 22 prizes in a 2021 raffle that also included drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán’s former safe house, homes, land and a luxury box at Estadio Azteca. The money raised was to support federal social programs, such as assistance for Olympic and Paralympic athletes.

More than 773,000 tickets sold nationwide for 250 pesos each (about US $12.60 at that time), and a woman from Jojutla in southern Morelos won the ranch.

However, Nereida Morales declined to take possession, citing the ranch’s deterioration and the maintenance costs. She later agreed to sell the property to the Morelos government for an undisclosed price.

The property was valued at 61.43 million pesos (US $3.1 million) for the lottery drawing.

Valdez, 53, was born in Laredo, Texas, in 1973. Nicknamed “La Barbie” for his blond hair and blue eyes, he was arrested in Mexico in 2010 and extradited to the United States in 2015.

He pleaded guilty to four drug-trafficking counts and one money-laundering count and in 2018 was sentenced to 49 years and one month in federal prison.

Court records later showed that Valdez had provided information to U.S. authorities while he was still a trafficker, including allegations that officials in former President Felipe Calderón’s administration had aided drug cartels.

In 2022, the Bureau of Prisons said Valdez was no longer in its custody but declined to disclose his location. That prompted speculation he was cooperating with U.S. authorities, but officials never confirmed that. A 2025 Justice Department release continued to list his 49-year sentence.

With reports from Animal Político and Diario de Morelos

World.title: What is President Sheinbaum’s view on Mexico becoming a data center hub?
World.content:
As data centers proliferate in Mexico, President Sheinbaum has taken a nuanced stand that recognizes the need for the centers but is skeptical about the country becoming a hub for them.

During her Tuesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum said she believes Mexico needs data centers to develop artificial intelligence (AI) but opposes becoming a “global data center” to meet external demand.

“We do need to have data centers to advance in artificial intelligence, but Mexico does not necessarily have to be the data center for other parts of the world, because it requires high energy and water consumption,” Sheinbaum said.

In Querétaro — which continues to lead AI expansion in Mexico — the debate has intensified precisely due to the potential pressure on strategic resources.

When asked about alleged power outages that had stalled data center investments in Querétaro, Sheinbaum cited reports from the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) showing such complaints have decreased. She also noted that investment is needed primarily in transmission and distribution, rather than in generation.

New data center facilities continue to arrive in the state, as well as in other parts of the country.

Indeed, according to market research firm Arizton, by January of this year, Mexico hosted some 47 data centers, mainly located in Querétaro, Mexico City and Guanajuato, with 12 more in the pipeline.

Just last week, KIO Data Centers announced it would invest up to US $1.3 billion to develop a new data center in Querétaro with the objective of meeting regional demand for cloud and AI infrastructure.

Although Sheinbaum acknowledged that data centers play an important role in the country’s modernization, their contribution to employment is low and their environmental impact is high.

“[Data centers] do generate economic growth, but with very little job creation and high consumption of natural resources,” Sheinbaum said, adding that her government is also prioritizing other sectors, such as manufacturing, which generate more jobs and place less pressure on natural resources.

Sheinbaum stressed that Mexico should develop the data centers it needs for AI through careful planning that considers the country’s technology needs, electricity infrastructure, natural resource constraints and job creation, rather than be driven by global demand.

With reports from La Jornada and Infobae

World.title: 9 alleged CJNG members arrested in Michoacán security operation
World.content:
Federal security forces on Wednesday arrested nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) in Michoacán. Among those detained was one woman identified as the daughter of a CJNG regional boss and another woman identified as the partner of the same man.

The CJNG responded to the federal operation by blocking highways in Michoacán at more than 20 points, including by setting vehicles on fire, but most, if not all, of the narco-blockades had been cleared by early Wednesday afternoon.

The Ministry of National Defense (Defensa) said in a statement that “nine members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel” were arrested in Tinaja de Vargas and Colesio, towns in the municipalities of Tanhuato and Ecuandureo, respectively. Those municipalities are located in northwestern Michoacán near the state’s border with Jalisco.

Defensa said that Mexican Army special forces and the National Guard carried out the operation in Michoacán “in coordination with” the federal Security Ministry, the Federal Attorney General’s Office and the Mexican Navy. Military intelligence work facilitated the location of the suspects.

Defensa said that Marisol “N” and Lourdes “N” were among the nine people arrested. The ministry said that the former has been identified as a daughter of Heraclio “N” (Heraclio Guerrero Martínez) while the latter has been identified as his “romantic partner.”

Defensa said that Guerrero, known as “Tío Lako,” is a CJNG “regional boss” in Michoacán and Jalisco. It also said he is “responsible for ordering attacks on National Guard troops” on Feb. 22, 2026, after the arrest of former CJNG leader Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, who was fatally wounded by military personnel during the operation to capture him.

Wednesday morning’s operation apparently targeted Guerrero, but the alleged cartel boss managed to avoid arrest.

Defensa said that two properties were secured during the operation and authorities seized 64 vehicles, one of which was armored; five machine guns; nine long guns; a handgun; two grenade launcher attachments; ammunition and magazines; drugs; eight improvised explosive devices; seven motorcycles; a drone; and tactical equipment.

The ministry said that the nine detained suspects were flown by a Mexican Air Force helicopter to Mexico City, where they were handed over to the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

Narco-blockades in Michoacán

Defensa noted that there were “various interruptions” to highways in Michoacán after the nine alleged CJNG members were arrested. Civilian and military authorities consequently activated “the Anti-blockade Plan” in order to “guarantee freedom of movement” in the state, the ministry said.

Presumed cartel members set up narco-blockades on highways in various municipalities of Michoacán, including Morelia, Zamora, La Piedad, Chilchota and Ecuandureo. Vehicles, including trucks and buses, were set on fire to create the blockades. Criminal groups in Mexico often create narco-blockades to impede security forces. The setting alight of vehicles is also a show of force for cartels as well as a demonstration of their anger over the arrest of one or more of their members.

⭕️ Al menos 12 bloqueos carreteros con vehículos incendiados fueron reportados en diez municipios de #Michoacán, informaron fuentes policiacas. Los cierres iniciaron alrededor de las 6:00 horas, tras un operativo de fuerzas federales contra un presunto líder del cártel Jalisco… pic.twitter.com/DQMz6bpZB2 — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) August 19, 2026

Michoacán’s C5 security command center reported on social media that 26 blockades set up in Michoacán on Wednesday morning had been cleared by 12:30 p.m.

Earlier in the day, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez noted that blockades at nine different locations had been cleared.

“We’re maintaining a permanent presence on the highways to guarantee your safety and to keep traffic moving smoothly,” he wrote on X.

“I ask that you drive carefully, follow the instructions of authorities, and consult only official sources,” Ramírez said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: García Harfuch earns DEA administrator’s praise at anti-drug trafficking conference
World.content:
Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Administrator Terrance “Terry” Cole publicly praised Security Minister Omar García Harfuch during this week’s 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference (IDEC) in Buenos Aires, Argentina, describing him as a “trusted partner” and a “good friend of the United States.”

Addressing representatives from more than 100 countries, Cole gave an overview of García Harfuch’s career with the Federal Police, Mexico’s Criminal Investigation Agency (AIC) and the Mexico City Security Ministry, prior to leading the Security and Citizen Protection Ministry. “Secretary Harfuch has devoted nearly two decades to public service to protect people in Mexico,” he said.

🤝🇲🇽🇺🇸 “García Harfuch es socio de confianza y buen amigo de Estados Unidos”. – Terry Cole / Administrador de la DEA #SegurosJuntos 🛡️🤝 pic.twitter.com/gYr6hupAfd — Embajada de EE.UU. en México (@USEmbassyMEX) August 19, 2026

Cole highlighted that the Mexican official is personally familiar with the risks of combating transnational criminal organizations, recalling the attack by the CJNG that he survived in June 2020.

He also noted that García Harfuch understands the importance of sharing intelligence, targeting criminal leaders, disrupting supply chains and dismantling networks from the top down.

In a separate speech, García Harfuch addressed the collaboration between the two countries, under which U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants for extradition purposes related to investigations by agencies in the neighboring country.

He said that 14 individuals — either wanted or considered priority targets by the FBI — have been arrested in connection with investigations into drug trafficking, homicide, money laundering, human trafficking and other activities of transnational criminal organizations.

Regarding financial matters, García Harfuch stated that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has added more than 2,300 subjects to its List of Blocked Persons, frozen over 8.6 billion pesos in assets (US $507 million) and blocked more than 24,600 accounts.

He also seized the international opportunity to share the numbers resulting from his ministry’s push to reduce violent crime over the past two years: 63,500 people arrested for high-impact crimes, more than 32,800 firearms seized and 518 metric tonnes of drugs confiscated. The number of daily homicides has dropped from 86 to 42, a more than 50% reduction.

En Buenos Aires, Argentina, me encuentro participando en la Conferencia Internacional para el Control de Drogas, donde compartimos los resultados de la Estrategia Nacional de Seguridad que encabeza la Presidenta @Claudiashein y que ha fortalecido las capacidades de inteligencia,… pic.twitter.com/kqGn1H6gpX — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) August 18, 2026

From his official X account, García Harfuch posted images of his participation in the Buenos Aires conference and reiterated Mexico’s commitment against international crime.

“Mexico will continue to cooperate with its international partners based on clear principles: shared responsibility, reciprocity, mutual trust and full respect for our sovereignty,” he said.

With reports from Imagen and Proceso

World.title: Mexico is fighting a US antidumping tariff on strawberries
World.content:
Mexico has condemned the U.S. Commerce Department for calling for an antidumping tariff on Mexican strawberries, a move Mexico says would violate international standards and threaten to end decades of largely duty-free strawberry trade between the two countries.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard voiced a “grave concern” over a preliminary determination by the U.S. that Mexican strawberry exports were being dumped during the winter season, which, if true, would constitute an unfair trade practice that consists of exporting goods at prices below their production cost or lower than the sales price in the domestic market.

Mexico’s Economy Ministry (SE) issued a statement Tuesday night informing the public that the U.S. accused Mexico of selling strawberries at prices between 3.37% and 5.28% below the normal product value.

To win the case, the U.S. must prove that Mexican strawberry sales are being made below fair value and the International Trade Commission (ITC), an independent quasi-judicial U.S. entity, must agree that the imports could cause material injury to the U.S. industry.

However, Mexico’s SE says that the “arbitrarily applied” U.S. criteria are inconsistent with the ITC Antidumping Agreement and with provisions in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

The case originated on Dec. 31, 2025, when Florida producers requested that the Commerce Department and the ITC impose antidumping duties, based on a differentiation between “strawberries” and “winter strawberries” harvested between Nov. 1 and March 31 and on the existence of a regional market limited to the eastern U.S. states.

The ITC concluded in March that there was no basis for considering winter strawberries as a distinct product from strawberries in general, nor for recognizing a regional market separate from the U.S. national market, according to Mexico’s Economy Ministry. But that conclusion was preliminary and did not halt the proceedings. The final ruling by the ITC is expected in early 2027, either allowing the U.S. to impose antidumping tariffs on Mexico or dismissing the case.

The imposition of tariffs would affect almost 5,000 Mexican strawberry producers — 97% of whom are small or medium-sized, with no more than 10 hectares — and around 151,000 jobs. In 2025, Mexico exported 263,000 metric tons of strawberries to the United States, valued at $1 billion.

On the other hand, from a U.S. industry perspective, Mexican producers are selling winter-harvested strawberries in the United States at prices U.S. producers cannot compete with.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has warned that the U.S. Commerce Department’s determination could set a precedent for other U.S. producers to challenge other Mexican fruit and vegetable exports by dividing products into seasons or delimiting regional markets.

According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, 98% of U.S. strawberry imports came from Mexico last year. Mexico accounts for 5.9% of global strawberry production, making it the world’s fifth-largest producer.

With reports from El Economista, Expansión, Infobae, CNN and Hortidaily

World.title: Why don’t more foreign tourists come to Central Mexico? MND’s journalism intern explains
World.content:
Nine weeks ago I set out on a mission. I had just arrived in Mexico for a journalism internship in San Miguel de Allende, and was trying to figure out why more foreigners — especially Americans — don’t travel to Central Mexico, and if they should.

Americans make up the majority of international arrivals into Mexico, but most head for the pristine coastline in Cancún, Cabo and Puerto Vallarta. Very few head to the country’s high-elevation center, and even fewer head to places outside of Mexico City.

But they are undoubtedly missing out. Americans tend to make long-haul trips to Europe to eat unique food, explore cobblestone streets and take in thousands of years of history. They can get the same experience with their southern neighbor, so why don’t they come?

Here are some of the reasons I found after living in Mexico for two months.

1. Public perceptions towards Mexico

The most obvious reason is the media perception of Mexico in the United States. Mexico is routinely painted as a hot, dangerous and drug-filled desert that sends millions of illegal immigrants through the northern border.

On Aug. 4, influencer César Gastélum was shot and killed on a live stream in Sinaloa amid ongoing cartel turf wars. The clip spread rapidly on social media, with the most-liked comments all calling Mexico unsafe and warning people to stay away.

Even before I started my internship, I had to go through weeks of safety training. I had friends tell me that they were scared for me and almost everyone questioned if it would be safe. That is the perception of Mexico that many Americans have.

Thirteen of Mexico’s 32 states have a level 3 or 4 advisory by the U.S. State Department, with only two — Campeche and Yucatán — holding a level 1 warning. These warnings and constant headlines of violence in Mexico keep the country off countless American bucket lists.

Mexico has problems, of course. Mexico’s homicide rate is 3-5 times higher than that of the U.S. and organized crime has plagued many states and areas around the country. But Mexico is a giant nation. There are parts I will never set foot in out of fear and parts I already want to go back to.

I grew up in the north suburbs of Chicago. Up there it is perfectly safe. Other parts of the city are not. There are areas of Chicago that I have never been to in my life, and that I never plan to go to. It is the same in Mexico but on a national scale. I will avoid Sinaloa and Ecatepec, but go to Mexico City and Oaxaca. Chicago and Mexico are both victims of clickbait headlines about widespread violence. Don’t believe them. I felt safer in Mexico than near my university in Seattle.

Wherever I went, I saw families playing outside and parties in town squares. The people seemed happy and secure. I do not get that same feeling in many parts of the United States.

2. Less familiarity

When most Americans think of an international vacation, they think of Rome, London, Madrid or Athens. Guanajuato, Querétaro, San Miguel de Allende or Oaxaca usually never cross their minds. There is a long history of Americans crossing the Atlantic for their big vacation, but that does not happen in Central Mexico.

While I met plenty of people who had been to San Miguel before I left, most had never even heard of it, let alone Guanajuato or Querétaro, which get far fewer American visitors.

Americans tend to like to enjoy places where they can be more comfortable, which usually means they flock to where Americans already are. Massive European hubs that have been recommended by countless American tourists to their friends and family will rake in visitors, while Central Mexican destinations — for better or worse — go unnoticed.

Central Mexico will never appear in as many movies (in a positive way, at least) as France or England. It will never be considered as romantic as Italy. So Americans will keep going to Europe.

I’ve been to Europe several times and now I’ve been to Mexico for nine weeks. The lack of familiarity, which is both real and exaggerated, is what made traveling in Mexico so great. I was never craving uniquely American experiences in Mexico. Why would I come to Mexico if I wanted everything to be like the United States?

So yes, there is sometimes a lack of familiarity. I noticed people wearing different clothes and eating different foods. They had different phrases that sometimes made me uncomfortable and they had different customs. But now I understand them and can go back to the U.S. having learned new things. I would not have gotten that if I just went to a place where every person I saw was a tourist.

3. Logistical and language issues

Americans like to speak English. In Central Mexico it’s far more common for people to lead with Spanish, unlike in Cabo or Cancún. For many American travelers, that’s enough to dissuade a visit.

Airport announcements are exclusively in Spanish, as well as signs at bus terminals. Sometimes asking for directions or ordering at a restaurant can be difficult. It can be hard to make conversation or meet acquaintances.

That’s part of the reason why San Miguel gets so many American tourists. You can easily get around with English and the town is relatively well-integrated to Americans. It may sometimes make for a less authentic trip, but one that is much easier to navigate and is more familiar while still having all the charm that Central Mexico provides.

As someone who speaks very limited Spanish, I was worried about the language barrier. Staying in San Miguel made it more seamless, but it was harder to get by when I traveled to Querétaro or Oaxaca. But that discomfort is part of traveling and part of becoming integrated in the culture. I had translation apps on my phone and tried to make an effort to speak in Spanish when I could. That was more than enough to get by.

It often was not easy but it was never that hard. If Spanish is stopping you from taking a trip to Mexico, I’m here to tell you that it shouldn’t. I struggled at times, but without trying to speak Spanish, I would not have been able to experience some of the rewarding experiences that I had.

What you’re missing out on

Colorful cities. Colonial streets. Winding mountain passes and waterfalls. Ancient ruins and cactus gardens. Tacos, tlayudas and empanadas.

Central Mexico truly has it all. I have been grateful to discover it during my nine-week internship. There were many times that I was grateful for streets that felt devoid of Americans, and there were times I was wishing for more familiarity. But that is the beauty of studying abroad.

Americans are missing out on many of the same experiences they can get in Europe. In Mexico, they can travel on a shorter flight and at lower prices. It also comes with learning what the real Mexico is like, which is ever-important as the two countries have been increasingly linked for decades. Over 38 million people of Mexican origin live in the U.S., and nearly two million Americans live in Mexico.

As these two countries seemingly grow apart over political tensions, meeting Mexicans in person and seeing how they truly live their lives has never been so fulfilling. It has also never been so maddening as they continue to be vilified in the United States. I can confidently say that coming to Mexico will be one of the greatest experiences of my college years and one that I will never forget.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups
World.content:
Thank you to everyone who completed the Mexico News Daily “Mexico and My Money” survey, which sought to gather information about the financial practices and experiences of foreigners living in Mexico.

Almost 700 of you responded to the survey and we have now analyzed the results, which are presented in this article.

Before we get to them, let us remind you that we conducted this survey to help guide and define the topics of a new MND series called “Mexico and My Money.”

The first article in the series, which was introduced by MND CEO Travis Bembenek earlier this month, will be published next week.

The MND ‘Mexico and My Money’ survey results

Who responded?

By our cutoff time, 680 people living in 25 of Mexico’s 32 states had responded to the survey.

The top 10 states where respondents live are Jalisco, Guanajuato, Nayarit, Quintana Roo, Baja California Sur, Mexico City, Yucatán, Oaxaca, Baja California and Sinaloa.

Around 44% of respondents have lived in Mexico for 11 years or longer, while the remaining 56% have lived here for 10 years or less.

The respondents are both full-time (70%) and part-time (30%) residents of Mexico.

Almost eight in ten respondents (79%) are retired, while the remainder work either part-time (11%) or full-time (10%).

More than seven in 10 respondents (73%) own their primary home, while the remainder rent.

10 Key Takeaways

7 in 10 respondents think their money is safe or very safe in banks in Mexico

More than four in 10 respondents (44%) think their money is “safe” in a bank in Mexico while an additional 28% believe their money is “very safe” in a bank in Mexico.

Almost one-quarter of respondents (23.5%) chose the “neutral” option in response to the question about the safety of their deposits in banks in Mexico.

Only 5% of respondents think their money is “unsafe” (4.5%) or “very unsafe” (less than 0.5%) in a bank in Mexico.

One factor that may have influenced people’s perceptions about the safety of their money in banks in Mexico is that federal Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora promptly reassured CIBanco and Intercam account holders that their money was “absolutely” safe after the U.S. Department of the Treasury last year accused the banks of laundering millions of dollars for drug cartels, prompting the government to take control of them. For the vast majority of CIBanco and Intercam customers that proved to be the case, although account holders who responded to a previous Mexico News Daily survey did face a range of inconveniences linked to the U.S. accusations.

8 in 10 respondents don’t have a Mexican credit card

Almost 37% of respondents don’t have a checking account based in Mexico, 58% don’t have a savings account with a bank in Mexico and a striking 79% don’t have a credit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

A strong majority of respondents (72%) do, however, have a debit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

The results suggest that many foreigners in Mexico use credit cards issued by banks in their countries of origin.

One possible reason why many foreigners opt not to get a credit card from a bank in Mexico is that credit card interest rates are typically very high.

8 of 10 respondents have made some kind of investment in Mexico

Only 21% of respondents have not invested in at least one of real estate, stocks, bonds or a business in Mexico. The remaining 79% of surveyed foreigners have invested in at least one of those assets.

The purchase of a home in Mexico was easily the most popular investment. Seven in 10 respondents (71%) own a home in Mexico, while 14% have a property in which they don’t currently live. Just over 12% of respondents receive rental income from a property they own in Mexico.

One in 10 respondents (10%) has invested in a business in Mexico, while 8% of surveyed foreigners have bought stocks and 9% have purchased bonds.

A strong majority of respondents have not had ‘money issues’ with contractors or other service providers in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (83%) of respondents have not had “money issues” with contractors in Mexico.

Almost nine in 10 surveyed foreigners (87%) have not had “money issues” with people who provide regular services to them in Mexico, such as landlords, cleaners or gardeners.

* Read about some of the money issues respondents have experienced with contractors and other service providers in the final section of this article.

Most respondents have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (82%) have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico, whereas 18% of survey respondents have been a victim of such an offense.

* Read about some of the financial crimes respondents have suffered in the final section of this article.

The vast majority of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico

Almost 97% of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico. Just over 3% of surveyed foreigners have borrowed money in Mexico.

This result suggests that the vast majority of respondents purchased real estate, vehicles and other assets in Mexico with their own funds or took out loans abroad.

As is the case with credit cards, the high cost of credit in Mexico is a deterrent to taking out loans in Mexico for many foreigners.

Rising prices in Mexico have negatively affected the lifestyles of 4 in 10 respondents

The increase in prices in Mexico in recent years has negatively affected the lifestyles of around four in ten (38%) respondents.

The lifestyles of the remaining 62% of surveyed foreigners have not been adversely affected by rising prices.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate fell to 3.12% in July, the lowest level in more than six years. However, inflation in Mexico was much higher in earlier years of this decade, peaking at an annual headline rate of 8.7% August and September of 2022.

Inflation, combined with other factors such as the strength of the peso, has made life in Mexico considerably more expensive in recent years.

Respondents are, on average, ‘somewhat concerned’ about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate

MND asked survey respondents to rate their concern over fluctuations in the value of the Mexican peso or the US dollar on a scale of 0 to 100.

On the scale, 0 meant “unconcerned”; 50 signified “somewhat concerned”; and 100 denoted “always concerned.”

The average response among respondents was 53, indicating that the surveyed foreigners are, collectively speaking, “somewhat concerned” about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate.

In general, fluctuations in the exchange rate are more of a concern now for foreigners in Mexico than in years gone by because, over a period spanning decades, the value of the peso against the US dollar trended down. However, in recent years the peso has bucked that trend, appreciating more than 10% against the greenback between 2021 and 2025, and continuing to strengthen this year.

A majority of respondents have loaned money in Mexico

Over half of the survey respondents have loaned money locally while living in Mexico.

Around 22% of respondents have loaned an amount under US $500, while 20% have lent between $500 and $3,000. About 11.5% of respondents have lent over $3,000 to someone in Mexico. Those three percentages add up to about 53.5%.

The remaining 46.5% of surveyed foreigners haven’t lent money to anyone while living in Mexico.

15% is the most common restaurant tip rate among respondents

Almost 48% of respondents typically tip “roughly 15%” of their total bill at restaurants in Mexico.

Almost 30% of surveyed foreigners usually tip “roughly 20%” when eating out, while 18.5% typically leave gratuities of “roughly 10%” of their total bill.

Just over 2% of respondents typically tip more than 20% of their total restaurant bill, while just under 2% usually tip less than 10%.

Your say

We asked survey respondents to provide additional information if they have experienced money issues with contractors and/or service providers in Mexico or if they have been a victim of a financial crime here. Many of the survey respondents who said they have been a victim of a financial crime recounted stories of being mugged, pickpocketed or having money stolen from their homes.

Below is a (lightly edited) selection of the comments we received.

Money issues with contractors

I paid for materials I didn’t get.

The price changed during the project due to the number of man-hours worked.

I had disagreements over what was included with certain construction costs. The disagreements arose from familiarity with what is typical in the U.S. versus what is typical in Mexico.

I paid for products and services I never received.

I didn’t receive reimbursement for a shoddy job.

I paid upfront for work that never happened or was executed poorly.

The contractor demanded more money than we agreed on.

The contractor failed to complete work and stole building materials.

Money issues with contractors and providers of regular services

A cleaning lady we had for eight years was stealing money from our purse and wallets during the whole time she was working for us.

A landlord kept my 20,000-peso security deposit without cause.

In order to continue having hot water in the apartment, I had to purchase equipment and pay for the installation because the landlord would not.

My rent increased above the agreed-upon rate. The increase was much higher than the standard rate increase in San Miguel de Allende.

The gardener wanted more money and simply stopped working until he got his raise.

I’m a former timeshare owner and the maintenance fee was immediately doubled after I was informed it was being adjusted because it was unfair. This was almost 20 years ago. It was extremely intimidating and I was threatened. Now that we know about cartel involvement in timeshares, I am so glad we got out even though we had to pay US $10,000.

My landlord insisted on me paying rent in US dollars, then stopped when the dollar weakened. The landlord greatly increased my rent, specifically saying, “My expenses have gone up because of inflation and the dollar isn’t worth as much.” She then converted the rent from dollars into pesos, increasing it by 20%.

I have had minor issues but have always been able to work them out. That’s life anywhere.

Financial crimes in Mexico

I was a victim of fraud when purchasing a car.

I was mugged. I lost my phone and wallet.

I was robbed of money, jewelry and a tablet by a “nurse” taking care of me.

Someone hacked my virtual HSBC card and ran up unauthorized charges.

I was the victim of the fraudulent sale of a timeshare.

An employee of a Mexican bank was siphoning funds and using new deposits to cover withdrawals. She was caught. I had to testify against her in exchange for the bank honoring my account balance.

I was coerced into a timeshare purchase.

A vacation rental that I paid for in advance was not owned or managed by the guy who rented it to me.

I was a victim of a credit card scam in a taxi.

A fruit vendor gave me counterfeit money.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Peso punches below 17 to the US dollar for the second time in a week
World.content:
Listen to this article

Buoyed by a weaker greenback, the Mexican peso appreciated on Wednesday morning to trade below 17 to the US dollar.

At midday Mexico City time, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 16.97, according to Bloomberg.

Earlier on Wednesday, the peso reached 16.95 to the dollar, its strongest position since June 2024. Compared to the Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate of 17.06 on Tuesday, the peso appreciated 0.65% to reach 16.95 to the dollar.

Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote on X that the peso appreciated on Wednesday morning due to “the weakness of the dollar” as a result of the U.S. Treasury Department’s announcement that it was increasing a bond buyback operation. The dollar weakened after the Treasury Department announced in a statement that it was “increasing, by at least double, the size of liquidity support buyback operations for longer-dated nominal coupon securities (the 10-year to 20-year sector and the 20-year to 30-year sector).”

At midday, the US Dollar Index, which measures the greenback against a basket of foreign currencies, was down 0.7% compared to the closing level on Tuesday.

Janneth Quiroz, director of economic analysis at the Monex financial group, said that the peso benefited from “the retreat of the dollar” and from the United States’ decision on Tuesday to pause planned 50% tariffs on almost $30 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The appreciation of the peso on Wednesday morning came after the currency broke the 17-unit-per-dollar floor last Friday morning. However, the peso closed at 17.03 to the dollar on Friday, according to the Bank of Mexico, and was also above 17 at the end of trading on Monday and Tuesday.

The peso has appreciated around 6% against the dollar so far this year after ending 2025 at 18.00 to the greenback.

In the most recent MND Peso Index™ analysis, which was conducted in early August when the USD:MXN rate was 17.22, the peso was found to be overvalued against the dollar by 2.4%.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Colombia Economic Emergency Declared After Deadly Earthquake
World.content:
Colombia · Economy

Key Facts — The decree Decree 1261 of 19 August 2026 declares a state of economic, social and ecological emergency.

— The scope Fifteen departments are covered, for 30 days, after a quake that touched 471 municipalities.

— The toll 314 dead, 4,437 injured and 262 missing, with 262,154 people counted as affected.

— The powers The president and his ministers can now issue decrees that carry the force of law.

— The check Every one of those decrees goes to the Constitutional Court automatically.

The last president who tried this had his decree thrown out by Colombia’s Constitutional Court. Which now gets an automatic look at this one.

Illustrative photo: Casa de Nariño, the presidential palace in Bogotá, where Colombia’s emergency decrees are signed. Decree 1261 of 2026 was signed there on 19 August. (Photo: Miguel Olaya from Bogotá, Colombia, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The Colombia economic emergency stopped being a plan on Wednesday night and became law. President Abelardo De la Espriella signed Decree 1261 of 2026, invoking Article 215 of the constitution after the earthquake of 10 August.

The measure runs for 30 days and covers 15 departments.

What Colombia Just Signed

For more than a week the government had said an emergency was coming. On Wednesday 19 August it finally arrived, in the form of a signed decree published by the presidency.

Decree 1261 of 2026 declares a state of economic, social and ecological emergency because of grave public calamity. The Colombia economic emergency is grounded in Article 215, the constitution’s emergency clause.

Inside the Colombia Economic Emergency Decree

The decree names 15 departments: Antioquia, Caldas, Cauca, Chocó, Quindío, Cundinamarca, Risaralda, Huila and Valle del Cauca. It also covers Tolima, Putumayo, Norte de Santander, Bolívar, Nariño and Sucre.

Other towns can be added later if they can show real damage. In all, 471 municipalities have reported some level of harm from the quake and its aftershocks.

The decree itself sets the rules of the game rather than the spending. Because of that, the concrete measures will arrive over the coming days as separate decrees.

Why the First Disaster Decree Was Not Enough

Colombia already had an emergency instrument in place. Decree 1171, signed on 11 August, declared a national disaster situation for 12 months under the country’s ordinary risk-management law.

That tool unlocked the national disaster fund and faster contracting. However, it could not change tax rules, rewrite budgets or create new legal obligations.

Article 215 can do all of those things. That is why the government reached for the heavier instrument once the scale of the damage became clear.

What Article 215 Actually Allows

Under Article 215 the president, signing alongside every minister, may issue decrees with the force of law. Each declaration lasts up to 30 days, and the total cannot pass 90 days in one calendar year.

Those decrees must relate directly to the crisis. In practice they can move budget lines, create funds, authorise direct contracting and change tax calendars.

The government may also impose temporary taxes. Still, such taxes lapse at the end of the following fiscal year unless Congress votes to keep them.

Where the Money Is Expected to Come From

Reporting on the decree points to credit, budget reallocation and royalties rather than a broad tax rise. Resources from the national royalties system can be redirected toward reconstruction.

The package is also expected to include rental subsidies, looser housing-subsidy rules and financial relief for households and firms. Employment protection and emergency contracting mechanisms are on the list too.

De la Espriella took office on 7 August, two days before the earthquake. He campaigned on freezing public spending and scrapping the wealth tax.

So a large tax increase would sit badly with his own promises.

The Human Numbers Behind the Paperwork

The balance circulating with the decree put the death toll at 314, with 4,437 injured and 262 people still missing. Some 262,154 Colombians were counted as affected.

One later report, citing the disaster agency’s own records, gave 319 dead and 260 missing. The counts move almost daily, since search teams are still working and registries are still being reconciled.

The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 7:34 in the morning on 10 August. Its epicentre was San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó.

The Constitutional Court Now Has the Last Word

This is the part investors will watch. The decree orders the text sent to the Constitutional Court the next day.

Requires a report to Congress and notifies the United Nations and the OAS. Review is automatic, not optional.

The court examines both the declaration itself and every decree issued under it. That review has bite.

In April 2026 the same court struck down the fiscal emergency that Gustavo Petro’s government had declared in December 2025. Ruling that the situation did not meet the constitution’s high bar.

Is This Really the Twelfth in Thirty Years?

A figure doing the rounds says Colombia has used Article 215 only 12 times in 30 years. That number is real but old, and it comes from an academic tally covering 1991 to 2011.

More recent counts do not match it. Colombian outlets have variously put the total at seven or nine over the past three decades, depending on what they include.

There have also been fresh declarations since, including one earlier in 2026. In short, treat the twelve-in-thirty-years line with care.

What Happens Next

Expect a wave of implementing decrees within days, covering housing, health, education, transport and infrastructure. Each will be tested against the same constitutional standard.

Congress keeps a political check as well. It may modify or repeal emergency measures during the year that follows the declaration.

Meanwhile the rebuilding bill keeps growing. Colombia’s planning department has sketched a reconstruction cost of up to US$12.9 billion.

Well above the earlier damage estimate of roughly US$9.6 billion.

Why It Matters Beyond Colombia

Emergency powers are a fast way to spend money and a fast way to lose control of it. Colombia has learned both lessons, most painfully in the disaster agency’s own recent corruption scandals.

For foreign residents, investors and companies, the practical effect is simple. Rules on contracting, taxes and permits in the affected departments can change quickly over the next month.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has the Colombia economic emergency actually been declared?

Yes. President Abelardo De la Espriella signed Decree 1261 of 2026 on 19 August, and the presidency published it.

How long does the emergency last?

Thirty days. Article 215 also caps all such declarations at 90 days within a single calendar year.

Can the government raise taxes under it?

It can create temporary taxes. However, they expire at the end of the next fiscal year unless Congress makes them permanent.

Could the decree be overturned?

Yes. The Constitutional Court reviews it automatically, and in April 2026 it struck down a previous emergency decree.

Sources: Infobae; Deutsche Welle; Noticias RCN; El Espectador; EFE; UNGRD.

World.title: Kenya’s KCB Opens a Five-Year Green Bond Programme in October
World.content:
Kenya · FINANCE

Key Facts Programme size KCB Group has launched a KSh 300 billion medium-term note programme under a new Sustainability Bond Framework, to be raised over five years.

KCB Group has launched a KSh 300 billion medium-term note programme under a new Sustainability Bond Framework, to be raised over five years. First tranche Up to KSh 100 billion is expected in October 2026, subject to regulatory approval following the framework launch on August 19, 2026.

Up to KSh 100 billion is expected in October 2026, subject to regulatory approval following the framework launch on August 19, 2026. Use of proceeds Funds are ring-fenced for green, blue and social projects, including renewable energy, clean transportation, affordable housing and MSME financing.

Funds are ring-fenced for green, blue and social projects, including renewable energy, clean transportation, affordable housing and MSME financing. Market backdrop In August 2026, the Central Bank of Kenya accepted KSh 312.03 billion in bids for reopened infrastructure bonds, more than double the KSh 150 billion on offer.

In August 2026, the Central Bank of Kenya accepted KSh 312.03 billion in bids for reopened infrastructure bonds, more than double the KSh 150 billion on offer. Parallel initiative Kenya’s Treasury is separately planning KSh 300 billion in road bonds, with a first tranche of KSh 175 billion to clear pending contractor bills.

Kenya’s Treasury is separately planning KSh 300 billion in road bonds, with a first tranche of KSh 175 billion to clear pending contractor bills. Issuer profile KCB Group is Kenya’s largest bank by assets and operates across multiple East African markets.

KCB Group, Kenya’s largest bank by assets, will float the first tranche of its KSh 300 billion sustainability bond programme in October 2026, targeting up to KSh 100 billion for green, blue and social projects.

KCB to float first tranche of a Sh300 billion programme bond sale in October (Photo: Internet reproduction)

What the KCB sustainability bond programme involves

KCB Group announced the medium-term note programme on August 19, 2026, under a newly launched Sustainability Bond Framework. The framework sets out how proceeds will be ring-fenced for eligible green, blue and social projects.

The bank plans to raise KSh 300 billion over five years, with the first tranche of up to KSh 100 billion expected in October, pending regulatory approvals. The instrument is structured as a sustainability bond, aligning with global environmental, social and governance taxonomies to attract both local and international investors.

Eligible uses include renewable energy, green buildings, clean transportation, sustainable water management, agriculture, blue economy projects, affordable housing and financing for micro, small and medium enterprises. The framework also targets support for women- and youth-led enterprises.

Kenya’s domestic debt market shows deep investor appetite

The KCB sustainability bond arrives against a backdrop of aggressive domestic bond issuance by the Kenyan state. In late July and August 2026, the Central Bank of Kenya reopened three tax-free infrastructure bonds with coupons ranging from 11.75 percent to 12.737 percent.

The offer size was KSh 150 billion, with the sale period running from July 30 to August 12, 2026. Bids reached KSh 460.4 billion, more than three times the amount on offer, and the central bank accepted KSh 312.03 billion, equivalent to about 208 percent of the initial offer.

After redemptions, net new borrowing stood at approximately KSh 193.9 billion. The strong demand for quasi-sovereign paper at yields above 11 percent signals deep domestic liquidity that KCB can tap for its corporate sustainability notes.

The road bond parallel and debt accounting tensions

KCB’s programme runs alongside a separate government-backed road bond initiative also targeting KSh 300 billion. The Treasury plans to issue road bonds backed by a dedication of KSh 12 of every KSh 25 per litre of petrol or diesel through the Road Maintenance Levy Fund.

The first tranche of KSh 175 billion would clear pending bills to road contractors, with a second bond of about KSh 125 billion covering future contractor bills. A KSh 104 billion bridge loan from a syndicate including KCB Bank Kenya, Absa Bank Kenya and UBA Kenya Bank would be funded by the first tranche.

Treasury officials and the International Monetary Fund reportedly differ on whether securitised arrears via a special purpose vehicle should count as sovereign debt. This disagreement matters for investors pricing KCB-linked exposures and sovereign risk when evaluating new bond programmes.

Why the KCB sustainability bond matters beyond Kenya

The KCB sustainability bond is part of a broader rewiring of African finance, where governments and major banks seek local-currency, capital-market solutions as Eurobond access tightens. Kenya’s recent issuance patterns show a clear strategy to lean more on domestic investors, including pension funds and insurance firms.

By adding an environmental, social and governance label, KCB can attract regional and global investors who are constrained from holding pure sovereign risk or who seek development-aligned impact with reasonable yields. The framework becomes a normative gateway, with external ESG metrics influencing local project selection.

This home-market pivot fits a wider continental pattern. African issuers are moving away from volatile, dollar-denominated Eurobonds towards structured local-currency instruments backed by earmarked revenue streams or ESG frameworks, a dynamic explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

Where the money goes and who benefits

The eligible project list maps directly to strategic sectors in African development. Renewable energy and green buildings are key to lowering Kenya’s carbon intensity, while clean transportation investments are classic arenas of great-power competition.

China has financed Standard Gauge Railway lines across East Africa, while Western and Gulf investors target ports, logistics and electric vehicle ecosystems. KCB’s bond adds local-currency depth to these projects, reducing dependence on external sovereign loans.

Financing for micro, small and medium enterprises, women- and youth-led businesses reflects a developmental agenda that harnesses private capital for inclusive growth. The more ESG rating agencies reward inclusive finance, the more banks like KCB allocate capital to these segments.

What to watch next

The first KCB sustainability bond tranche is expected in October 2026, subject to regulatory approval. Investors will watch pricing against sovereign curves, where infrastructure bonds currently offer coupons above 11 percent.

The Central Bank of Kenya’s bond switch auctions also continue, with the bank inviting holders of short-term Treasury bills and a 15-year bond maturing in 2027 to switch into a 10-year bond maturing in November 2029. The aim is to raise KSh 15 billion while extending duration in a high-rate environment.

The road bond securitisation debate with the International Monetary Fund will also shape how investors perceive Kenya’s true debt exposure. If obligations are shifted off-balance sheet, bondholders may misprice risk, affecting demand for both sovereign and corporate paper.

What is being sold, and what is not

The KSh300 billion figure is the ceiling of a medium-term note programme running over five years. It is not a single bond and it is not being issued at once.

The first tranche is planned at up to KSh100 billion. That is the part that actually reaches investors this year.

Anyone reading that Kenya has sold a KSh300 billion green bond has read it wrong. The programme has been launched; the paper has not been placed.

The distinction matters for anyone pricing Kenyan bank credit off the headline.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will KCB float the first tranche of its sustainability bond? KCB Group expects to issue the first tranche of up to KSh 100 billion in October 2026, subject to regulatory approval. What will the KCB sustainability bond proceeds be used for? Proceeds are ring-fenced for green, blue and social projects, including renewable energy, clean transportation, affordable housing, agriculture and MSME financing. How large is KCB Group’s overall sustainability bond programme? The medium-term note programme totals KSh 300 billion to be raised over five years under the bank’s new Sustainability Bond Framework.

Connected Coverage For more on how African issuers are reshaping continental finance through local-currency instruments and ESG frameworks, read Africa: The New Scramble.

World.title: Nigeria Shuts an Insurer That Could Not Raise Enough Capital
World.content:
Nigeria · FINANCE

Key Facts Licence revoked The National Insurance Commission cancelled Universal Insurance Plc’s operating licence effective 14 August 2026.

The National Insurance Commission cancelled Universal Insurance Plc’s operating licence effective 14 August 2026. Shareholder loss BusinessDay estimates shareholders stand to lose about ₦13.6 billion as the stock becomes worthless.

BusinessDay estimates shareholders stand to lose about ₦13.6 billion as the stock becomes worthless. Liquidator named Ogbonna Chukwumerije of Pinheiro LP was appointed receiver and provisional liquidator.

Ogbonna Chukwumerije of Pinheiro LP was appointed receiver and provisional liquidator. Regulatory deadline All insurers had to meet new minimum capital requirements by 30 July 2026 under the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025.

All insurers had to meet new minimum capital requirements by 30 July 2026 under the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025. Sector survivors NAICOM said 43 insurance and reinsurance companies met the new capital rules and would receive new licences.

NAICOM said 43 insurance and reinsurance companies met the new capital rules and would receive new licences. Policy goal The reform is tied to President Bola Tinubu’s target of a US$1 trillion Nigerian economy by 2030.

Nigeria’s National Insurance Commission has revoked the Universal Insurance licence effective 14 August 2026 after the company failed to meet new minimum capital requirements, triggering liquidation and leaving shareholders facing losses of about ₦13.6 billion.

NAICOM revokes Universal Insurance licence over failure to meet recapitalisation requirement (Photo: Internet reproduction)

What happened to the Universal Insurance licence

The National Insurance Commission, known as NAICOM, announced it had cancelled the operating licence of Universal Insurance Plc and begun winding-up proceedings. The regulator appointed Ogbonna Chukwumerije of Pinheiro LP, a Nigerian law firm, as receiver and provisional liquidator.

NAICOM said the company failed to raise capital to the minimum level required for its licence category within the compliance period. The revocation means Universal Insurance can no longer write new business, and its shares typically suspend or collapse on the Nigerian Exchange.

BusinessDay estimates that shareholders stand to lose about ₦13.6 billion, describing the revocation as turning Universal Insurance stock into worthless paper. The company’s assets and liabilities now fall under the liquidator’s control for creditor-first resolution.

The recapitalisation rules behind the crackdown

The Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act, known as NIIRA 2025, was signed into law by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu on 31 July 2025. It launched a 12-month recapitalisation exercise requiring all insurers and reinsurers to comply with new Minimum Capital Requirements by 30 July 2026.

The new thresholds are steep. Life insurers must hold at least ₦10 billion in capital, non-life insurers ₦15 billion, composite insurers ₦25 billion, and reinsurers ₦35 billion.

NAICOM’s circular warned that any company failing to meet the prescribed minimum within the timeframe would face liquidation, merger, or other resolution actions. The regulator also introduced a risk-based capital framework and engaged KPMG, Deloitte, EY and PwC to verify insurers’ capital positions.

Universal Insurance’s failed capital raise

Before the revocation, Universal Insurance had obtained shareholder approval for a ₦15 billion capital raise designed to meet the new non-life threshold. The company also entered a binding investment agreement with FPNG Co-Nvest Limited for a ₦7.128 billion injection via private placement.

The board said the deal, combined with other measures, would enable the company to exceed its regulatory capital requirements. Despite these steps, NAICOM’s final verdict was that Universal Insurance did not meet the prescribed minimum within the stipulated timeframe.

The company is one of eight insurers whose licences have been revoked for failing recapitalisation tests. Others include Staco Insurance, Goldlink Insurance, Nigeria Re, NICON Insurance, African Alliance Insurance Plc, Nigerian Agricultural Insurance Corporation and Royal Exchange Prudential Life Plc.

Winners and losers in Nigeria’s insurance shake-out

On 2 August 2026, NAICOM announced the successful completion of the 12-month recapitalisation exercise. The regulator said 43 insurance and reinsurance companies had met the new minimum capital requirements and would receive new licences.

A further eight insurers that submitted evidence of compliance close to the deadline were placed under final verification and regulatory review. That review was expected to be completed within 14 days.

Analysts describe a power shift in Nigeria’s insurance market, with well-capitalised groups consolidating share while weaker legacy firms are forced into mergers or liquidation. The big four audit firms gain lucrative verification mandates, while prominent lawyers are positioned as receivers in high-value insolvencies.

The political economy of insurance reform

NAICOM states explicitly that the recapitalisation exercise is part of President Tinubu’s financial sector transformation agenda aimed at achieving a US$1 trillion Nigerian economy by 2030. By raising capital requirements, the government hopes to deepen domestic savings pools and boost insurers’ capacity to underwrite major infrastructure projects.

The reform also carries political economy risks. New capital vehicles like FPNG Co-Nvest emerge as potential consolidators, inviting scrutiny over whether recapitalisation is also a redistribution of control over insurance assets to politically connected investors.

For policyholders, NAICOM stresses that revocation does not automatically extinguish valid claims. Customers are advised to document policies and claims, engage with the liquidator, and monitor announcements as the winding-up proceeds.

What to watch next in Nigeria’s insurance sector

The fate of the eight insurers under final verification will shape the sector’s near-term structure. Their approval or rejection will determine whether the market consolidates further or stabilises at the 43 already verified companies.

The liquidation of Universal Insurance and Nigeria Re will test how quickly policyholders and creditors recover value. The process will also reveal whether the appointed liquidators can realise assets efficiently in a market with limited distressed-asset experience.

Broader questions remain about who ultimately controls the recapitalised insurers. The emergence of new investors such as FPNG Co-Nvest, alongside the big four auditors’ verification role, suggests the reform is as much about reallocating corporate control as it is about prudential standards. This fits the wider pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble, where financial reform intersects with competition for influence over African markets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did NAICOM revoke Universal Insurance’s licence? NAICOM revoked the licence because Universal Insurance failed to raise capital to the minimum level required for its licence category within the compliance period under the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025. How much money will Universal Insurance shareholders lose? BusinessDay estimates shareholders stand to lose about ₦13.6 billion as the licence revocation turns Universal Insurance stock into worthless paper. What happens to Universal Insurance policyholders now? Policyholders and creditors are expected to lodge claims with the appointed liquidator, Ogbonna Chukwumerije of Pinheiro LP, who will realise assets and settle legitimate claims to the extent available.

A chat-first off-ramp for everyday crypto users

MYPADI AI, stylised as MyPadi AI, was founded by Nigerian tech entrepreneur Yakubu Quadri and launched in May 2026. Quadri positions the product as a way to simplify crypto transactions across Africa.

The entire experience lives inside WhatsApp chat, with no separate mobile app or exchange dashboard. Users begin by sending “Hi MyPadi” on WhatsApp, after which the chatbot guides them through identity verification and automatically creates wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Ethereum and USDT.

Once verified, users can check balances, convert crypto to fiat and withdraw to bank accounts by chatting with the AI assistant. The platform markets itself with the line “No apps, no complexity. Just chat with MyPadi,” and emphasises that no vendor sits in the middle of transactions.

Security features include secure KYC, multi-layer authentication, PIN verification for each transaction and WhatsApp end-to-end encryption. The company also cites secure API integrations and blockchain-level verification as part of its enterprise-grade security approach.

Why Nigeria’s crypto economy needs a better cash-out path

Nigeria combines high crypto adoption with currency instability and a history of regulatory clampdowns on informal foreign exchange channels. Crypto and stablecoins have become tools for hedging against naira depreciation, receiving payment for digital work from abroad and moving money across borders.

Historically, Nigerian users cashed out through peer-to-peer marketplaces or informal vendors who took crypto and paid naira at opaque rates. That model is operationally complex and risky, with recurring stories of fraud, failed settlements and frozen accounts.

MYPADI AI explicitly references “the single biggest risk that has burned so many Nigerian crypto users in the past” and pitches a vendor-less off-ramp instead. Users send crypto to system-managed wallets, and the platform handles conversion and bank transfer under the hood.

This positions MYPADI AI as part of a second wave of African crypto infrastructure that abstracts away wallets, exchanges and peer-to-peer marketplaces. The goal is to turn off-ramping into a familiar messaging-based experience rather than a technical chore.

WhatsApp becomes Africa’s de facto money interface

WhatsApp is Africa’s dominant communications platform, with ecosystem materials citing over 200 million active African users daily. For many users, especially in informal and low-income segments, WhatsApp is the default interface for business, remittances and social life.

Downloading and learning a new finance app is a high-friction step that many users simply skip. MYPADI AI and peers such as Azza take the view that crypto rails should sit inside existing messaging habits rather than requiring new software.

Azza, built by Nigerian-based USEAZZA, is another WhatsApp-based, AI-powered crypto wallet and on/off-ramp. It supports buying, selling, swapping and cashing out crypto via chat, with fiat support for Ethiopian birr, Nigerian naira, Kenyan shilling, South African rand, Ugandan shilling, Ghanaian cedi and CFA franc zones in various stages of roll-out.

Building on WhatsApp means African fintech products like MYPADI AI are structurally dependent on Meta, a United States-owned platform. Access, APIs and future monetisation are subject to Meta’s policy decisions, which are themselves shaped by US and European regulatory environments.

Competition and the wider WhatsApp crypto stack

Nigeria’s crypto market already includes exchanges such as Busha, Roqqu and Quidax, which offer advanced trading features and multi-asset support. These services depend on users downloading apps and managing custodial or non-custodial wallets.

MYPADI AI’s bet is that mass-market cash-out demand will be won by the product closest to users’ everyday apps. The platform is off-ramp-first, focused on conversion from crypto to fiat and direct bank settlement rather than speculative trading.

Azza is active in Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa, with confirmed expansion plans to Ghana, Singapore and Argentina. It currently allows selling crypto for Nigerian naira or Kenyan shilling, with broader fiat support in development and USDT-to-USD conversions into dollar-denominated domiciliary accounts.

Together, these products form an emerging WhatsApp-native finance layer across Africa. Nigerian founders are experimenting with how far messaging-based agents can replace traditional banking user experience for everyday money movement.

The state, stablecoins and the great-power angle

The Nigerian Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy launched an Artificial Intelligence Research Scheme in October 2023. The scheme planned to fund 45 startups and research consortia, each with 5 million naira in grants, to build an AI ecosystem across finance, agriculture, governance and health.

MYPADI AI fits the government’s stated interest in AI in finance and local innovation that can drive digital inclusion. But the product also brings crypto cash-out into KYC-compliant, bank-linked channels, which is attractive to regulators who prefer traceable rails.

At the same time, the service operates over end-to-end encrypted messaging, where transaction logic is opaque to the state except through bank and exchange records. This duality, more traceable at the bank level and more private at the messaging layer, will likely be a point of contest in Nigeria’s regulatory debate over AI agents and chat-based finance.

The core assets, Bitcoin, Ethereum and USDT, anchor African users to dollar-denominated crypto instruments even when they interact in naira or rand. This creates what can be described as shadow dollarisation via WhatsApp, with US-regulated stablecoin issuers and US-owned platforms quietly pulling African financial activity into the dollar’s orbit. The broader pattern fits the themes tracked in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

MYPADI AI reported processing over 2 million South African rand in secure ZAR settlements as of August 2026. The company describes itself as “Built from Africa, for the way Africans actually move money,” underscoring its focus on remittances and day-to-day payments rather than purely investment speculation.

The key question is whether Nigerian regulators will embrace chat-based off-ramps as compliant alternatives to informal peer-to-peer markets or scrutinise them as new vectors for capital flight. The answer will shape how quickly products like MYPADI AI scale beyond early adopters.

Another variable is Meta’s willingness to support financial services built on WhatsApp in African markets. Any change to API access, encryption policy or monetisation rules could alter the economics of the entire WhatsApp-native finance layer.

For now, MYPADI AI represents a concrete experiment in turning Africa’s most-used messaging app into a quiet clearing house for crypto-to-fiat conversion. Its success or failure will offer an early signal of whether chat-based finance can move from novelty to mainstream utility.

A number worth treating carefully

Coverage of Nigerian fintech routinely says WhatsApp has more than 200 million daily users in Africa. Meta does not publish that figure.

Meta reports 3.60 billion daily active people across all its apps for June 2026, and gives no regional breakdown for WhatsApp at all.

The African number is a third-party estimate assembled from country-level survey data. It is a reasonable order of magnitude and it is not a company disclosure.

That does not weaken the business case. It does mean the headline number in most write-ups has no primary source behind it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is MYPADI AI and when did it launch? MYPADI AI is a WhatsApp-based crypto off-ramp founded by Nigerian tech entrepreneur Yakubu Quadri that launched in May 2026. It lets users convert Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether USDT into Nigerian naira and South African rand directly through WhatsApp chat. How does MYPADI AI differ from Nigerian crypto exchanges like Busha or Quidax? MYPADI AI lives entirely inside WhatsApp and focuses on off-ramping crypto to fiat with direct bank settlement, rather than offering a trading dashboard. It removes peer-to-peer vendors from transactions, which the company says reduces counterparty risk for everyday users. Which currencies and crypto assets does MYPADI AI support? MYPADI AI supports Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether USDT as crypto assets. Users can convert these into Nigerian naira and South African rand, with funds paid straight into bank accounts.
