World.title: Trump put thousands of soldiers on Washington’s streets. They seldom stop crime
World.content:
NATIONAL GUARD. Members of the National Guard walk inside the Lincoln Memorial, after US President Donald Trump deployed the force and ordered an increased presence of federal law enforcement to assist in crime prevention, in Washington, D.C., US, August 18, 2025.

Soldiers mostly responded to incidents in wealthier, whiter areas and were absent from neighborhoods where 82% of murders take place

WASHINGTON, USA – Well past midnight one day this spring, three police officers pulled up to a nightclub where a man was stomping on a young woman lying on the sidewalk.

The officers stopped the attack and arrested him, according to a police report. It was the kind of assault police might encounter on almost any night in almost any city.

But one detail stood out to police officer Xavier Jimenez, who wrote the report: “There was approximately 15 national guard members in the area on routine patrol who did not take any action.”

President Donald Trump deployed thousands of National Guard troops to Washington last summer as the centerpiece of what he describes as a no-holds-barred effort to combat crime, especially in cities run by Democrats. Every day, small clots of soldiers in camouflage and body armor patrol tourist-heavy areas of the US capital, including national monuments, subway stations and the area around its professional baseball park.

What the soldiers seldom do, Reuters found, is fight crime.

Since their arrival last August, the National Guard soldiers Trump ordered to Washington have been mentioned in only a tiny fraction — about 1.3% — of the criminal cases filed in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, which handles nearly all the city’s criminal prosecutions. In dozens of cases, the soldiers appear not as people making the arrests but as victims of crime.

The roughly 4,500 soldiers currently deployed to Washington outnumber its 3,200 police officers. And they cost more: The Trump administration last year told Congress that sending guardsmen to the capital cost about $1.65 million a day — before officials doubled the number of troops this summer. The city’s most recent police budget was about $1.5 million daily.

The administration told Congress it plans to keep sending soldiers to Washington — though it has not said how many — until the end of Trump’s presidency in 2029 at a cost of $1.4 billion.

To gauge the impact of that deployment, Reuters reviewed every publicly available charging document filed in Superior Court and interviewed lawyers, residents, service members and others who are familiar with their work.

The soldiers mostly responded to minor incidents in neighborhoods that are wealthier, whiter and less dangerous than the rest of the capital, Reuters found after comparing court records to the city’s demographics and crime information. Reuters could find no reference in court records to soldiers doing any kind of law enforcement in the neighborhoods where about 82% of the city’s 859 murders occurred over the past five years.

The White House did not respond to questions about soldiers’ work. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump’s efforts in the city have “driven down crime, beautified the city, and improved quality of life for countless individuals.”

DC Mayor Muriel Bowser, who has called the deployment “problematic,” declined to comment, as did the city’s police department.

The National Guard taskforce managing the Washington deployment did not respond to questions about its work or its cost. A spokeswoman, Leona Hendrickson, said soldiers were too busy to be interviewed.

Although soldiers have sometimes broken up fights or assaults, many of the crimes for which they detained people have been minor. In October, soldiers chased down a man who had taken two slices of pizza and offered $2 as partial payment, according to police records. A week later, they stopped a man who threw a rock at a bus. In April, they detained a man who allegedly stole two beef jerky sticks worth about $7 from a pharmacy, according to the report. Last month, six soldiers held a woman who drank a bottle of root beer without paying.

The Rev. William Young, who lives in the Navy Yard neighborhood where soldiers patrol frequently, laughed when asked whether the troops made him feel safer. “It’s a way of keeping fear in all of us,” he said. “This is not how a capital of democracy should be protected, by having soldiers marching to protect the streets.”

‘They could have done more’

Reuters found 217 criminal cases in Washington in which police mentioned the involvement of the National Guard. In about a quarter of them, 62 cases, soldiers single-handedly stopped people suspected of a crime, often for things like shoplifting or jumping turnstiles to avoid paying subway fare. In another 43 cases, soldiers helped police officers arrest someone.

Videos obtained by community groups also show troops in groups of 20 or more stationed outside subway stations at night, blocking teens from descending the escalators to enforce a city curfew.

“It’s like they brought people here from all across the country, just to be here. And they harass people a lot more than they are actually doing police work,” said the Rev. Norman Nixon, the pastor of the Union Temple Baptist Church.

Although the guardsmen have been deputized as US Marshals, according to government records, they have limited law-enforcement power. The Defense Department has described their work as “presence patrols,” a show of force meant to deter crime rather than respond to it. They can detain suspects, but then must call police officers to make a formal arrest.

Court records describe 35 instances in which the troops were witnesses to crimes, sometimes simply watching until police officers arrived. They have told officers about a drug deal, a man urinating in public, another who exposed himself to a subway policeman and two men writing with chalk on a monument outside the city’s train station, one of them wearing a banana costume.

Evelyn Jones said she wonders whether soldiers could have saved her nephew, Keon Jones, who was stabbed to death in April near a trendy strip of hotels and restaurants on the city’s waterfront.

The soldiers called emergency services after finding Jones unresponsive after a fight. They later told police they thought Jones was merely intoxicated. They did not realize, until after officers reached the scene, that he had been stabbed so severely his intestines were spilling out. He died in hospital about two hours later.

“They could have done more to help him,” his aunt said.

The service members themselves have often been victims, a fact underscored last year when two soldiers from West Virginia were shot not far from the White House, killing one of them.

Reuters found 62 cases in which people were charged with pushing, punching or threatening soldiers. Nine were accused of spitting on the soldiers. One man allegedly tried to grab a soldier’s pistol as the soldier tried to arrest him for stealing baseball caps in a subway station. Another man was charged after he told a group of soldiers that he wanted to “shoot you, in between your balls, with a bazooka,” according to a police report.

And twice, police in Washington arrested off-duty soldiers for violating the city’s firearms laws, though the US Attorney’s Office dropped the charges against both of them.

This summer, they took on a new mission: guarding the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which the Trump administration spent millions of dollars to renovate only to see it turn green with algae as its liner peeled away. Trump claimed the pool was sabotaged by vandals. But U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro eventually conceded that a government contractor “botched” the job.

Patroling safer neighborhoods

The US has long used National Guard soldiers to respond to disasters, help secure major events like the Super Bowl and occasionally quell riots, but they haven’t been used for everyday crime-fighting. Trump also authorized smaller deployments in Memphis and New Orleans and has mused about sending soldiers to other cities.

“You do not want armed soldiers on the streets of America,” said Gen. Randy Manner, who retired in 2012 as the second-in-command of the National Guard Bureau. He said soldiers are ill-prepared for police work and more expensive than hiring more police officers.

Determining the soldiers’ impact on crime in Washington is not straightforward. In addition to the soldiers, the Trump administration sent hundreds of extra federal agents into the city, who largely functioned as local police officers.

The number of murders in Washington fell for the third consecutive year. But homicide numbers also dropped in cities where the government has not sent soldiers or additional federal agents. And the total number of violent crimes — serious assaults, robberies and sex offenses in addition to homicides — reported by city police between January and mid-August is marginally higher than last year, about 4%.

A study in May by the nonpartisan Niskanen Center found that sending soldiers into Washington led to fewer stolen cars but had no impact on violent crimes.

Charles Stimson, a senior fellow at the pro-Trump Heritage Foundation, said the soldiers’ visibility served as a deterrent. “When you’re speeding and you see a cop, you slow down,” he said. “If those National Guard went poof and left town tomorrow, crime would go up.”

The Reuters review of court records found little evidence of soldiers’ presence in high-crime neighborhoods where they might have responded to more serious crimes.

Instead, the court records show soldiers were more likely to be mentioned in arrest records in city neighborhoods that have higher incomes, in which more people have college degrees, and where more people are white. Most of the arrests in which soldiers participated were either near the city’s core or its subway stops.

Reuters used the location of incidents in court records to identify the areas in which soldiers were either assisting the police or seeking help from them, then compared those neighborhoods to the rest of the city. That does not account for places soldiers might have been sent if they did not interact with law enforcement there. But it suggests that their presence was not aimed at quelling the violent crime that had ravaged parts of the city in the past.

Salim Adofo, an outreach coordinator with the Anacostia Coordinating Council, a nonprofit operating in a low-income part of the city, said that matched his experience.

“I haven’t seen them all year,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: World View with Marites Vitug: Enrico Gloria on how countries negotiate with China
World.content:
Rappler editor-at-large Marites Vitug sits down with political scientist Enrico Gloria to discuss how China uses sanctions and diplomacy as foreign policy tools

Bookmark this page to catch the discussion on Friday, August 21, at 6 pm!

MANILA, Philippines – Relations between the Philippines and China remain strained as disputes increasingly extend beyond the West Philippine Sea.

While Beijing and Manila have kept communication channels open, recent incidents have exposed how difficult it is to negotiate even limited arrangements. This raises broader questions about how countries engage with one of the world’s most powerful states.

On Friday, August 21, Rappler editor-at-large Marites Vitug speaks to political scientist Enrico Gloria to unpack China’s approach to negotiations and how it uses both sanctions and diplomacy as foreign policy tools.

Gloria is an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman. His research focuses on China’s foreign policy, political discourse, and Philippines-China relations, among others.

What lessons can the Philippines draw from other countries that have negotiated with Beijing?

World.title: FACT CHECK: No ICC admission of being ‘paid’ by Marcos gov’t in Duterte case
World.content:
There is no statement, document, or credible report of the ICC supposedly admitting to colluding with the Marcos administration; the court has repeatedly reiterated that it operates independently

Claim: The International Criminal Court (ICC) admitted to being paid by the Marcos administration as part of a plan against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video uploaded by channel “BANAT KABAYAN TV” was titled “Hala! OMG! Kasabwat pala? Plano ni Marcos at ICC, nabulabog? Grabe ICC, umamin bayad wasak na?”

(Hala! OMG! They’re conspirators? Marcos and ICC’s plan exposed? Wow, ICC admitted to being paid, destroyed?)

Its thumbnail reads “Plano ng ICC, nabulabog! ICC, umamin bayad utos BBM?” (ICC’s plan exposed! ICC admitted being paid, ordered by BBM?), with the additional text “Nabuking sabwatan!” (Conspiracy exposed!)

As of writing, the video has garnered over 3,800 views and 288 likes.

The facts: There is no statement, document, or testimony from the ICC, the Philippine government, or any credible news outlet showing that the court admitted to receiving payments from the Marcos administration or that it supposedly acted on Marcos’ orders in its investigation of Duterte.

The video points to the Philippine government’s actions as evidence of an alleged alignment with the ICC. However, it provides no evidence of alleged payments or secret coordination. Instead, it discusses the ICC’s general funding, which comes from contributions by its member states.

While Philippine authorities facilitated Duterte’s arrest and transfer to the ICC in March 2025, Marcos asserted that it was in compliance with the country’s commitment to the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) — not as a scheme coordinated with the ICC.

The misleading video’s thumbnail also features former ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, whose involvement in Duterte’s case had already ended before the video was posted. Khan stepped aside from his duties in May 2025 pending an investigation and was withdrawn from the Duterte case in October 2025 over a conflict of interest. He was subsequently removed as ICC prosecutor due to sexual misconduct allegations.

No collusion with Marcos: The ICC has repeatedly rejected allegations that it was acting on behalf of the Marcos administration. Responding to Vice President Sara Duterte’s description of the tribunal as Marcos’ “lapdog,” ICC spokesperson Oriane Maillet told the Inquirer that the court operates independently and impartially under the Rome Statute.

In a separate interview, ICC spokesperson Fadi El Abdallah likewise stressed that the court is a judicial, not political, institution, saying its judges make decisions independently.

“These judges will only deliver justice. They don’t take any political considerations into account when they are deliberating about important judicial matters,” he said.

The ICC’s case against Duterte: Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity before the ICC, stemming from the alleged killings linked to the Philippine government’s bloody drug war during his presidency and his earlier tenure as Davao City mayor. The ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously confirmed the charges.

Although the Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute in 2019, the ICC retains jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed while the country was a member, covering the period from November 2011 to March 2019.

Duterte remains in ICC custody in The Hague. His case has since moved to the Trial Chamber, with the trial scheduled to open in November 2026. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: [OPINION] When a child can reach a gun
World.content:
This can only mean that someone has failed to secure it or a system has failed to stop its illicit journey. Trace every gun, close every leak.

As I write this, families and students in Zamboanga are confronting a grief that no school community should ever have to carry. Initial reports say that a junior high school student entered the Ateneo de Zamboanga University Junior High School campus with two guns, killed another student, and then died by suicide. The investigation is still developing. We should therefore speak carefully about motive, responsibility, and how the weapons were obtained.

What is already clear is that this tragedy came less than two months after the shooting at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, where three students were killed and 20 were injured. Two deadly school shootings in such a short period can no longer be dismissed as isolated events. Together, they demand a national response.

The immediate instinct will be to place more guards at school gates, inspect every bag, install metal detectors, and conduct active-shooter drills. Some of these measures may be necessary, especially where risk assessments identify clear vulnerabilities. Yet they begin at the final point in a much longer chain. By the time a child arrives at school carrying a gun, several systems have already failed.

A school shooting begins long before the first shot. It begins when a gun becomes accessible to a child.

For almost three decades, I have worked in humanitarian disarmament. Much of this work has involved landmines, cluster bombs, explosive remnants of war, small arms and light weapons, arms transfers, and the difficult task of persuading governments and armed groups to protect civilians.

One lesson has remained constant: a weapon causes harm through a chain of decisions. Someone manufactures it. Someone transfers it. Someone registers or conceals it. Someone stores it, carries it, lends it, loses it, sells it, or allows it to be diverted.

School shootings should be examined through the same life-cycle approach. We need to ask where the firearm came from, who legally or physically controlled it, how it left that person’s control, whether its loss was reported, where the ammunition came from, and which warning signs appeared before the child reached the campus.

Some weapons move through this chain lawfully until a moment of theft, negligent loss or deliberate diversion. Others enter through illicit manufacture, a paltik workshop, smuggling, an unauthorized transfer, an obliterated serial number, an online transaction, or the leakage of parts and ammunition. These are different pathways, but they lead to the same urgent question: who allowed the weapon to move closer to a child?

Informal networks

The Tacloban case made these questions impossible to avoid. Police reported that one firearm had been issued to a police officer, while another was registered to a private security agency. The investigation into the Zamboanga guns must establish its own facts. Still, both cases direct our attention upstream, toward the homes, armories, police units, security companies, gun clubs, workplaces, and informal networks through which children may gain access to weapons.

The Philippines already has a comprehensive guns law. Republic Act No. 10591 requires a vault, locked container, or other security measure for the safekeeping of guns. It also recognizes the problem of loose guns: unregistered, stolen, illegally manufactured or improperly held weapons, including guns with altered identification or revoked licenses.

Yet, the general storage requirement and existing criminal prohibitions have proved inadequate for the specific danger of child access and the fragmented pathways of illicit circulation. A container may technically be locked while its key remains easy to find. A service firearm may be brought home after duty.

A weapon may be treated as a familiar household object rather than as an instrument capable of ending several lives within seconds.

Responsibility must follow the firearm

The strongest policy response begins with a clear principle: if a child can reach a firearm, the firearm is inadequately secured or inadequately controlled, regardless of whether it is licensed, privately owned, company-owned, government-issued, stolen, diverted, locally fabricated or smuggled.

This principle shifts our attention from punishment after tragedy to responsibility before tragedy. A 14-year-old or 15-year-old may face consequences under the law and the child-protection system. Yet the adult or institution entrusted with the weapon must answer a more fundamental question: how did a child obtain effective control over it?

Every firearm in a home where a child lives or regularly visits should be unloaded and kept in a tamper-resistant safe.

Ammunition should be secured separately. Keys, passcodes, and biometric access must remain under the effective control of an authorized adult. Compliance should be verified when a licence or firearm registration is issued or renewed. For low-income licensed owners, government should provide subsidized safes and a reasonable assisted-compliance period.

When a child obtains an unsecured weapon, the owner’s licence should be suspended while the incident is investigated. When negligent storage results in injury or death, civil, administrative, and criminal accountability should follow in proportion to the owner’s conduct. These measures define the responsibilities that ownership carries when a lethal weapon is kept around children.

A higher standard should apply to police, military, and private security guns.

Weapons issued in the name of public safety should be subject to auditable issue-and-return records. They should return to an armory after duty unless a documented operational reason requires otherwise. Loss, theft, or unauthorized access should be reported immediately. When a government-issued or company-owned weapon reaches a child, an investigation independent of the custodian’s immediate unit should begin automatically.

Trace every gun, close every leak

Safe storage is indispensable, but safe storage alone reaches only guns that remain within a lawful and identifiable system. A child may encounter a gun that was never registered, was stolen years earlier, leaked from a police or security inventory, was assembled from illicit parts, or crossed a maritime route outside official control. Prevention must follow those weapons too.

Every firearm that reaches a child has a journey.

Government should require every gun seized, surrendered or recovered in a school-related incident to be safely recorded within twenty-four hours, forensically examined, tested against ballistic evidence, and traced from manufacture or lawful importation to the last identifiable custodian and suspected point of diversion. Restoring an obliterated serial number may reveal one part of that journey. Linking a recovered cartridge case to another crime may reveal another.

This work cannot belong to one police desk. It requires the PNP guns, investigation and forensic services to work with the National Bureau of Investigation, Bureau of Customs, Philippine Coast Guard, the Armed Forces of the Philippines, intelligence agencies, digital investigators and peace-process institutions. International cooperation through the Special Envoy on Transnational Crime, Philippine Center on Transnational Crime, INTERPOL, SOMTC on Combatting Arms Smuggling, and ASEANAPOL can help identify weapons reported lost, stolen, trafficked or smuggled elsewhere.

The aim should be to identify the leak, rather than merely count the arrest.

Was the firearm stolen from a household? Did a licence holder transfer it illegally? Did it disappear from an armory? Was it made in an illicit workshop or brought through a port? Who supplied the ammunition? A trace that ends with the last lawful owner but does not explain the diversion remains unfinished.

Community recovery and voluntary surrender can also remove loose guns from circulation, provided they are lawful, carefully designed and protected against coercion or planted evidence. Conflict-affected and Bangsamoro communities must never be treated as collectively suspect. Formal decommissioning and normalization arrangements under peace agreements deserve protection, while enforcement focuses on evidence, trafficking networks and actual diversion pathways.

The policy can be summarized in six words: trace every gun, close every leak.

Bantay-Baril sa Bata

I propose that Congress consolidate and strengthen the pending child firearm-access prevention measures into a Bantay-Baril sa Bata: Safe Homes, Safe Schools Act.

Its purpose would reach beyond declaring campuses gun-free. It would connect firearm custody, illicit-circulation disruption, child protection, school safety, mental health support, police responsibility, tracing, and judicial intervention.

One creative and necessary mechanism would be a Child Firearm Access Alert. Every school should have access to a small multidisciplinary team composed of the school head, guidance counsellor or psychologist, child-protection officer, social worker, and a specially trained police liaison. When credible information indicates planned violence, suicidal behavior, weapon-seeking, targeted retaliation, or another acute danger, the team should ask one direct question: Does this child have access to a firearm?

That question must cover access through a parent, relative, neighbor, police or military officer, security guard, gun club, workplace, illicit market, or another source. When credible access is identified, the team should be able to coordinate immediate safety planning with the family, health professionals, social services, and law enforcement.

In cases of imminent risk, a judge should be able to issue a short, reviewable Child Firearm Safety Order. The order could authorize the temporary deposit or securing of specifically identified guns for up to seventy-two hours, followed by notice and a prompt hearing if continued custody is sought. Due process, confidentiality, access to counsel, and penalties for malicious reports must be built into the procedure. The child and family should also receive appropriate support.

This is neither a permanent watchlist nor an invitation to label difficult, bullied, withdrawn, or mentally distressed children as dangerous. Threat assessment should focus on behavior, communications, circumstances, and actual access to weapons. Mental illness, video games, social media use, or experience of bullying cannot serve as automatic explanations for violence. Simplistic blame may satisfy the demand for a quick answer while leaving the firearm-access pathway untouched.

The Philippines should resist importing a model of school safety built mainly around fear and fortification. Schools need controlled entrances, trained guards, functioning communication systems, trauma-sensitive emergency procedures, first-aid equipment, and regular coordination with responders. They also need counsellors, credible anti-bullying systems, confidential reporting, restorative responses where safe, and pathways for urgent clinical care.

Teachers should never be armed. The routine display of weapons in classrooms would change the relationship between educators and students and increase the number of guns present in already stressful environments. A school should remain a place where a child can seek help before a crisis becomes violence.

Preparedness also requires honest learning after every incident. Each firearm recovered in connection with a school threat or shooting should be traced through its entire chain, whether it is licensed or loose: manufacture or import, registration or absence of registration, transfer, official issuance, custody, storage, theft or loss reporting, illicit manufacture or trafficking, ammunition source, diversion point, and access by the child. The public deserves redacted annual reporting on the source of these weapons, the failures identified, and the corrective actions taken. Children’s identities and sensitive operational information must remain protected.

The more meaningful response

There will be calls to lower the age of criminal responsibility. There will be calls to ban a game, censor a platform, arm teachers, or turn every school into a guarded compound.

These proposals offer visible action, but visibility is different from prevention. A child can be punished only after an adult, an institution, or an illicit network has already allowed a firearm to enter the child’s world.

The more difficult response is also the more meaningful one. It requires gun owners to accept enforceable duties. It requires police and security agencies to account for every issued weapon, while law-enforcement, customs and border authorities trace guns circulating beyond the licensed system. It requires schools to recognize warning signs without stigmatizing children. It requires judges, social workers, counsellors, health professionals, families, and law-enforcement officers to act together before danger becomes irreversible.

The deaths in Tacloban and Zamboanga should lead to more than temporary guards, hurried bag inspections, and expressions of grief. They should establish a durable national standard: every lawful firearm must remain under the effective control of the adult or institution responsible for it, and every illicit firearm recovered must be traced toward its source and diversion point. When custody or control fails, accountability must follow.

Perhaps the most important intervention will take place far from any classroom. It will occur when a gun is locked in a proper safe, a service weapon is returned to an armory, a missing firearm is immediately reported, an illicit shipment is intercepted, a recovered gun is traced, a community safely surrenders a loose weapon, or a court acts on credible information before a child reaches the school gate.

We cannot promise that violence will never happen again. We can refuse to leave guns within a child’s reach, or allow them to circulate without tracing, and call the result unforeseeable. Prevention begins with secure custody. It continues by tracing every gun and closing every leak. – Rappler.com



Fred Lubang is a Mindanaoan peace practitioner-scholar, regional representative of Nonviolence International Southeast Asia, and National Coordinator of the Philippine Campaign to Ban Landmines. He holds a PhD in Applied Conflict Transformation Studies and a recipient of the 2022 Seán MacBride Peace Prize.

World.title: Most Americans believe Trump has inappropriately profited since returning to power, poll finds
World.content:
TRUMP. US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters about the helipad being constructed on the South Lawn, at the White House in Washington, DC, U.S., August 19, 2026.

WASHINGTON, USA – A majority of Americans believe President Donald Trump and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since his return to power and that his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The four-day poll, completed on Monday, August 17, found that half of Trump’s own Republicans believe the president allows considerations for his business interests to influence his decisions, a striking finding for a leader who pledged to clean up corruption in Washington.

Trump was born into a New York real estate family and built his name into a globally recognized brand before running for office. He earned more than $1.4 billion last year from his family’s cryptocurrency ventures, including World Liberty Financial and the Trump meme coin, digital assets he has publicly championed. In March 2025, two months into his second term, the president called attention on social media to his self-branded crypto coin, describing it as the “Greatest of them all!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!”

Some 63% of respondents said it was inappropriate for Trump and his family to have profited in that way, while 32% said it was appropriate and the rest did not answer the question. About three in 10 Republican respondents called the deals inappropriate, while seven in 10 said they were appropriate.

Democrats regularly highlight alleged corruption in the administration ahead of the November midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years, while Trump’s administration has vowed to investigate alleged corruption in Democratic-run states.

Trump says that he has had no day-to-day role in his family’s business since returning to office and that his investments are independently managed. He has pursued crypto-friendly policies in his second term, after courting crypto cash ​on the ⁠campaign trail.

The White House dismissed any allegations of impropriety, saying Trump’s investments were managed by independent financial institutions.

“There are no conflicts of interest,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “The President only acts in the best interests of the American public.”

‘Nothing like this before’

But experts on presidential ethics called the current confluence of business and politics in the White House unprecedented.

“We have seen nothing like this before, even the first Trump administration did not have as many complex business interests as the second Trump administration,” said Richard Painter, the top ethics lawyer for Republican President George W. Bush.

Some 69% of Americans — including two-thirds of independents and nine in 10 Democrats — said they thought Trump’s private business interests were influencing his presidential decisions.

Americans are divided on whether corruption is worse under the Trump administration than under other recent presidents. Democrats largely think there is more graft, while Republicans are split roughly down the middle, with 56% thinking corruption is at least a little better and the rest thinking it is steady or worse.

“It’s concerning,” said Thomas Schmidt, a semi-retired crossing guard in Cudahy, Wisconsin, who voted for Trump in 2024 but has soured on the president this year. “He should be more concerned with his presidency than with his business practices.”

Schmidt said his biggest worries are about Trump’s inability to control inflation or extract the U.S. from the war with Iran that he helped start. He doesn’t think Trump is different from other presidents in mixing his business deals with politics. “I think every president’s done something like that.”

Trump campaigned ahead of his 2016 presidential victory on a promise to fight corruption in Washington, or “drain the swamp,” as he put it.

The public’s views of Trump’s personal enrichment could weigh on his party in the November midterm elections, which will determine who controls Congress during the last two years of his term. Americans say corruption is prevalent across all levels of government, with four in 10 Democrats saying they are extremely angry about graft, compared with one in four Republicans. When poll respondents were asked which party was more corrupt, 41% pointed to the Democratic Party and 49% to the Republican Party.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, surveyed 1,166 US adults nationwide between August 14 and August 17. The results had a margin of error of 3 percentage points for all Americans and 5 points for Democrats, Republicans and independents. – Rappler.com

World.title: ABS-CBN makes room for new owners
World.content:
Hours after a quiet annual meeting, ABS-CBN moved to triple its authorized capital and expand its board. The P6-billion rescue brings money without more debt, but at the price of diluting the owners already there.

The new investors were nowhere in sight when ABS-CBN Corp. held its virtual annual stockholders’ meeting Wednesday morning, August 19. By afternoon, the company had started making room for them. Hours after stockholders elected a 7-member board and adjourned an annual meeting whose agenda had been set before ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue was signed, the newly organized board proposed adding two more chairs around its own table. It also approved tripling the company’s authorized capital, creating enough shares for the investors putting fresh money into the wounded media company. Stockholders will be called back on September 30 to approve both changes.

The capital increase was expected. ABS-CBN has agreed to issue 1,643,835,616 new common shares in exchange for the P6 billion, but it simply does not have enough shares available today to give the investors. The two additional seats around the board table are more intriguing. ABS-CBN did not say who they are intended for, but their creation comes just a week after I&C Holdings Corp. agreed to put P3.5 billion into ABS-CBN, by far the biggest contribution to the rescue. Three Lopez family branches — Crème Investment Corp., Mantes Corp., and Presta Holdings Company Inc. — are putting in another P2.2 billion from personal resources, while Lopez Inc., the longtime controlling shareholder that sits at the apex of the Lopez empire structure, had earlier been identified as contributing another P300 million. It is therefore too early to say whether one or both new seats are being created for I&C, for representatives of the Lopez branches putting fresh money directly into ABS-CBN, or for someone else altogether.

What is clear is that a 7-member board elected Wednesday morning could become a 9-member board after the rescue, making the corporate math about much more than creating enough shares. The P6 billion will also redraw who owns how much of ABS-CBN, including the stake of the Lopez holding company that for decades sat comfortably in control.

Making room upstairs and downstairs

First, ABS-CBN has to create the shares. Its authorized capital stock is currently P1.5 billion, made up of 1.3 billion common shares at P1 par value each. With almost 900 million common shares already issued, there is not enough room under that limit to issue another 1.64 billion shares for the new investors. To fix this, the board approved increasing authorized capital stock threefold, from P1.5 billion to P4.5 billion. This raises the number of authorized common shares from 1.3 billion to 4.3 billion, while the one billion preferred shares stay the same. The higher limit gives ABS-CBN more flexibility than it immediately needs: even after issuing the 1.64 billion new shares, it will still have unissued shares available if it needs to raise more capital in the future.

ABS-CBN said the purpose of the amendment was to accommodate the new subscriptions of I&C, Crème, Mantes, and Presta. One name is conspicuously absent from that list: Lopez Inc., which had earlier been identified as contributing P300 million to the P6-billion rescue. Its omission from the August 19 disclosure needs clarification from ABS-CBN before conclusions can be drawn about whether its investment is being treated differently or has changed. But the company is not only making room in its capital structure. It is also proposing to make room around the table that governs it.

Only hours before proposing a 9-member board, ABS-CBN stockholders had elected 7 directors: chairman Martin Lopez, president and CEO Carlo Katigbak, Charo Santos-Concio, Federico “Piki” Lopez, Rafael Lopez, and independent directors Monico Jacob and Honorio Poblador IV. The three Lopez directors represent three branches of the family: Piki from the Oscar branch, Martin from the Manolo branch, and Rafael from the Geny branch. Rafael is the brother of former ABS-CBN chairman Gabby Lopez, whose branch recently sold its stake in Lopez Inc. There was no I&C representative among the 7, which was hardly surprising since the nomination and voting process for Wednesday’s annual meeting had been set in motion before I&C signed its subscription agreement. By afternoon, however, ABS-CBN was proposing two more seats, giving the company room to accommodate new representation without necessarily displacing any of the 7 directors stockholders had just elected.

But who gets those two chairs remains unanswered. I&C is the obvious party to watch because it is putting up P3.5 billion, more than half of the P6 billion rescue money, but Crème, Mantes, and Presta together are putting in another P2.2 billion directly from three Lopez family branches. ABS-CBN has disclosed neither the intended nominees for the additional seats nor any board representation rights negotiated with the investors. For now, the two chairs are empty. The two independent directors who left the board on Wednesday, Randy David and Emmanuel “Noel” de Dios, meanwhile remain inside ABS-CBN’s governance orbit: the new board appointed both to its Board of Advisors, alongside Cynthia del Castillo, Federico Garcia, Antonio Jose Periquet, former finance secretary Cesar Purisima, and Salvador Tirona, while Poblador was designated lead independent director.

The price of money

There was another way for P6 billion to enter ABS-CBN. The new investors could have advanced or lent the money to the company, avoiding the need to create 1.64 billion new shares, but that would also have added another obligation to a company already carrying billions of pesos in debt. Loans have to be repaid and generally carry interest that must be serviced whether or not the underlying business has recovered enough to make money.

ABS-CBN chose instead one of the most ordinary ways companies raise fresh capital: equity. The investors put money into ABS-CBN in exchange for newly issued shares and become owners themselves. Unlike lenders, equity investors do not expect the company to pay them contractual interest every month, quarter or year, nor does ABS-CBN eventually have to repay their P6 billion as loan principal.

Their return depends instead on what happens to the company they now partly own — whether the wounded business heals, turns around its dire financial situation, becomes profitable again and eventually produces returns through dividends or a more valuable stake.

For ABS-CBN, that means P6 billion of fresh capital without adding another P6 billion to an already heavy debt load. But equity has its own price: dilution.

ABS-CBN currently has almost 900 million common shares outstanding, and Lopez Inc. owns about 502 million of these, or roughly 55.8%, making it the majority shareholder before the new investment. Think of ownership as a fraction: Lopez Inc.’s shares are the numerator, while the total number of shares in the company is the denominator. When 1.64 billion new shares are added, the denominator grows sharply, but the numerator for each existing shareholder stays the same unless they buy more. Existing shareholders still own the same number of shares, but because the denominator has expanded, each share now represents a smaller slice of the company. This is dilution in simple terms: the pie gets bigger, but your slice does not, so your percentage shrinks. This means all current investors — including ordinary stock market buyers and major shareholders like Batangas representative Leandro Leviste and Lopez Inc. — end up owning a smaller percentage of ABS-CBN than before unless they increase their numerator by buying into the new offering.

Lopez Inc. is not standing still in this process. Its proposed P300 million fresh investment would soften that fall because it would receive new shares in return, increasing its own numerator as the denominator expands. And Lopez Inc. is not acting alone in the broader family ecosystem. Crème, Mantes, and Presta, representing three allied Lopez family branches putting another P2.2 billion directly into ABS-CBN. Taken together, and depending on final allocation and pricing, these related family investments could still leave the Lopez group collectively holding a majority stake in the expanded company (more than 50%, based on previous estimates by Rappler, read here), even as individual percentages shift sharply.

That said, Lopez Inc. on its own is still significantly diluted. A Rappler estimate puts Lopez Inc.’s post-transaction stake at only about 23%, underscoring how steep the dilution becomes once the full P6-billion equity round is taken up. The scale mismatch is clear: the P300 million accounts for only about 5% of the total infusion, even as Lopez Inc. enters the transaction as ABS-CBN’s 55.8% owner. If all P6 billion is ultimately subscribed at the same price, that additional investment will cushion its dilution but will not, by itself, preserve its majority stake. The final ownership percentages will still depend on the exact allocation and pricing of the new shares, which ABS-CBN has not yet fully disclosed.

That is the trade-off embedded in the rescue: instead of taking on another P6 billion in debt, ABS-CBN is effectively paying for its lifeline by giving up a much larger share of itself.

Why September 30?

None of these changes takes effect simply because the board wants them. Increasing ABS-CBN’s authorized capital and expanding its board require amendments to its Articles of Incorporation, with the capital increase requiring approval by stockholders representing at least two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock before going through the remaining regulatory process. ABS-CBN has scheduled that vote for September 30, with September 7 as the record date.

September 30 can feel like a long time away for a company urgently seeking fresh money, but a special stockholders’ meeting cannot simply be summoned the following morning. ABS-CBN has to determine which stockholders are entitled to vote, prepare the information explaining the proposed amendments, go through the required filing and notice process, give stockholders time to vote, secure the necessary approval and then take the amendments through the remaining Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) process. The timetable therefore shows how the corporate machinery has to catch up with a transaction assembled in August.

What makes September 30 more consequential is another clock already running inside ABS-CBN. The latest disclosed extension on its P5 billion BPI loan facility expires August 31, a month before the special meeting, while its P4.75 billion UnionBank loan runs until September 30, the very day stockholders vote. That coincidence should not be read to mean ABS-CBN automatically has to hand UnionBank P4.75 billion that day. ABS-CBN has been negotiating longer-term refinancing, and the lenders could extend, refinance or restructure the facilities again. But it exposes the different speeds at which ABS-CBN’s rescue is moving. The debt clock is running faster than the equity clock: BPI’s current deadline arrives before stockholders even vote on the capital increase, UnionBank’s falls on the day of the vote itself, and even a successful September 30 vote does not instantly put P6 billion into ABS-CBN’s bank account because the amendments and share issuance still have regulatory and other conditions to clear before the subscriptions can be completed.

Screenshots from ABS-CBN’s annual stockholders’ meeting on August 19, 2026.

ABS-CBN therefore still has to manage the old debt while it waits for the new equity, and the banks are not the only ones waiting. Former employees are still owed retirement and separation obligations after years of retrenchment, while suppliers, production costs, taxes, salaries and other accrued expenses are among roughly P12 billion in trade and other payables sitting on the group’s balance sheet as of June 30. The company has said the fresh capital will be used for working capital, strengthening the balance sheet and other general corporate purposes, but has not disclosed how the P6 billion will ultimately be divided. The fresh money, in other words, already has a line forming for it before it even arrives.

Making room

The timing captures the unusual place ABS-CBN now finds itself in. On Wednesday morning, stockholders gathered for an orderly, sanitized annual meeting built around the company and ownership structure that existed before the rescue. By afternoon, the board was already preparing for the one that comes after it.

The P6 billion buys ABS-CBN something its existing balance sheet badly needs: money without another layer of debt and interest payments. But the company is paying for that breathing room with ownership.

For decades, control of ABS-CBN was almost synonymous with Lopez Inc. After 1.64 billion new shares are issued, that will no longer be so simple. September 30 is when the old owners will be asked to formally make room for the new. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

Below are some of the author’s articles on the Lopez family saga:

World.title: What Kazakhstan’s Recent Elections Reveal About Voter Participation
World.content:
ASTANA – Voter turnout in Kazakhstan has fluctuated considerably in recent national elections, with presidential contests drawing higher participation than the two most recent parliamentary votes, as experts point to party mobilization, geography and public trust as key factors.

Turnout is not just how many people cast ballots. It can also offer insight into political engagement and parties’ ability to mobilize supporters, particularly in parliamentary elections centered on party competition.

Recent elections also suggest a difference between presidential and parliamentary contests. According to figures from the Central Election Commission, turnout reached 77.5% in the 2019 presidential election and 69.44% in the 2022 presidential vote, compared with 63.3% in the 2021 parliamentary election and 54.15% in the March 2023 parliamentary vote.

Aigul Sadvokasova, director of the Almaty-based Institute of Philosophy, Political Science, and Religious Studies, said presidential elections tend to generate greater voter participation because the choice is centered more directly on individual candidates. Parliamentary elections, by contrast, depend more heavily on voters’ interest in political parties and their platforms.

Sadvokasova made the comments during an Aug. 13 meeting of the Sailau-2026: The Nature of the Political Campaign expert platform in Almaty, organized by the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan.

Historically, national turnout figures also mask substantial regional differences.

For example, in the 2023 parliamentary election, participation varied sharply between Kazakhstan’s largest cities and several regions. Turnout ranged from 25.82% in Almaty to more than 60% in several regions.

Zhenisbek Tolen, head of the Center for Educational Sciences and Social Development at Kazakhstan’s National Academy of Sciences, said regional electorates should not be viewed as homogeneous. Voters in regional capitals and remote districts, as well as younger and older people and different occupational groups, can have significantly different priorities.

“A region is not a single voter. It is made up of different social groups, and a party’s success depends on how effectively a strong local team can speak to each of them in a language they understand,” Tolen said, addressing the expert meeting.

Sadvokasova said turnout is shaped by a broader set of factors, including where voters live, trust in political institutions, access to information, whether citizens feel they can influence political processes and how competitive they perceive an election to be.

Those factors may take on an important role in a parliamentary election. Under Kazakhstan’s current electoral system, all 145 Kurultai deputies are elected through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency, meaning voters choose a party rather than individual candidates within its list.

In a comment to The Astana Times, Riccardo Pelizzo, dean of Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Public Policy, also emphasized the role of mobilization. Election results, he said, reflect not only voter preferences but also whether parties can persuade their supporters to actually cast ballots.

According to Pelizzo, who discussed voter turnout and electoral participation on The Astana Times’ podcast earlier this year, electoral success depends on the “ability to mobilize voters, to bring voters to the polls and to have high turnout levels.”

The Astana Times has followed the race through weekly reviews, from the parties’ initial policy pitches and regional campaigning to the first televised debate, an education-focused debate, and the final campaign week’s focus on the rule of law.

Experts say the current campaign has unfolded in a more active information environment, with parties stepping up outreach to voters and making greater use of televised debates and digital communications. But visibility during a campaign does not automatically translate into participation. One of the central challenges for political parties is sustaining voters’ interest through election day.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election Attracts 777 Foreign Observers
World.content:
ASTANA – A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election, Central Election Commission (CEC) Secretary Mukhtar Yerman said on Aug. 18.

The figure includes 138 members of parliaments from 41 countries.

International monitoring

According to the CEC, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs submitted 121 observer candidates from 18 countries and five international organizations for accreditation.

The observers include representatives of the CIS Observer Mission, the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Turkic Academy.

National observers include representatives from Belgium, China, France, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Japan, Jordan, Mongolia, the Philippines, Serbia, Slovakia, Thailand, Türkiye, Turkmenistan, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Uzbekistan.

CEC Chairman Nurlan Abdirov said the presence of foreign observers contributes to the campaign’s openness and transparency and demonstrates Kazakhstan’s continued cooperation with foreign states and international organizations in the electoral sphere.

Representatives of the central election bodies of 22 countries are also taking part, including 11 heads of election commissions, he said.

First test of the new system

The election will be the first nationwide vote under Kazakhstan’s new parliamentary model. Citizens will elect 145 members of the Kurultai, a new unicameral Parliament, through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency.

Seven political parties are contesting the election. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to enter the legislature.

The new system replaces the previous bicameral Parliament and removes single-member constituencies from national parliamentary elections. The vote will therefore provide an early indication of how the redesigned system affects party competition, political representation and the composition of the legislature.

The campaign has also placed greater emphasis on party platforms. Nationally televised debates have focused on areas including agriculture, social policy, economic development, environmental protection and the rule of law.

Political observers have described the debates as a test of whether parties can present distinct policy positions and respond to public scrutiny.

What international observers will assess

The presence of international observers adds a separate layer of assessment to the election.

Their work will provide an external view of how the new electoral framework operates in practice. The monitoring will also contribute to broader international understanding of Kazakhstan’s parliamentary and electoral reforms.

The number of observers is therefore significant not only as a measure of international attention, but also as part of the transparency surrounding the first Kurultai election.

The election is scheduled for Aug. 23. Its immediate results will show which parties cross the 5% threshold and how the 145 seats are distributed.

The longer-term test will be how the new Kurultai functions under the redesigned parliamentary system and whether the changes strengthen political representation and institutional accountability.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Fertilizer Industry Could Strengthen Food Security and Export Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding domestic fertilizer production to reduce import dependence, support agriculture and develop higher-value exports. Major nitrogen and potassium projects planned by 2030 could help create a more complete domestic fertilizer industry.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has repeatedly stressed the importance of expanding domestic fertilizer production to reduce import dependence and develop export potential. Major investment projects in nitrogen and potassium fertilizers now support the policy, with new capacity planned by 2030.

Expanding domestic production

Mineral fertilizers are divided into nitrogen, phosphate and potassium groups. Kazakhstan has an established phosphate industry, while nitrogen and potassium production remain priorities, reported the Ministry of National Economy on Aug. 18.

The KazAzot Prime complex in the Mangystau Region is expected to produce 660,000 tons of ammonia, 577,500 tons of urea and 500,000 tons of ammonium nitrate annually. Its launch in 2030 would more than triple national ammonia capacity and create Kazakhstan’s first industrial-scale urea production, with around 700 permanent jobs.

The integrated model will also increase processing. Around 543,000 tons of ammonia will be used to produce urea and ammonium nitrate, creating greater value from domestic production.

From importer to exporter

Kazakhstan currently has no potassium fertilizer production, despite more than 6.6 billion tons of confirmed potassium salt reserves. Domestic demand of nearly 14,000 tons is therefore fully covered by imports.

The Qazaq Kalium project at the Satimola deposit plans to produce 1.5 million tons of potassium fertilizer annually by 2030. Even if domestic demand rises to 300,000 tons, most of the planned output could be exported.

KazAzot Prime also has significant export potential, with planned annual exports of approximately 470,000 tons of urea and 98,000 tons of ammonium nitrate. Export volumes are expected to use the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), or the Middle Corridor.

Rising domestic demand

Fertilizer use in Kazakhstan is increasing rapidly, from 679,000 tons in 2023 to 1.8 million tons in 2025. The 2026 target is 2.3 million tons, or up to 73% of scientifically justified demand.

Yet consumption remains below international levels. Kazakhstan applies an estimated 25-35 kilograms per hectare, compared with a global average of 150-160 kilograms. State compensation of up to 60% of fertilizer costs provides additional support for farmers.

A new export opportunity

Developing nitrogen, phosphate and potassium production could help Kazakhstan reduce imports while creating a new, higher-value export industry.

Key indicators will be completion of the planned projects, continued growth in domestic fertilizer use, and Kazakhstan’s ability to reach international markets through the Middle Corridor.

If these plans are implemented, fertilizers could become an important new pillar of Kazakhstan’s chemical industry, supporting food security while strengthening the country’s export portfolio.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Export Growth Signals Shift Toward Stronger Global Market Presence
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s foreign trade entered a stronger phase in January-June, with exports growing faster than imports and non-resource and processed goods gaining ground in major international markets. The key question is whether this represents a temporary improvement in trade performance or a stronger shift in the structure and geography of Kazakhstan’s exports.

Exports outpace imports

In January-June, Kazakhstan’s exports reached $40.3 billion, up 8.6% compared to a year earlier, while imports increased 5.4% to $31.5 billion. Total foreign trade turnover rose 7.2% to $71.8 billion, producing a positive trade balance of around $8.9 billion.

Faster export growth matters because it shows external demand is driving trade expansion more than imports. Exports increased by approximately $3.2 billion compared with the first half of 2025, while the overall trade balance remained firmly positive, reported the Ministry of Trade and Integration on Aug. 18.

Non-resource exports gain momentum

More important, however, is the performance of non-resource and processed goods. Their exports reached $15.2 billion, up 17.6% year on year. This was almost six times faster than the 3% growth in imports of the same category.

Compared with January-June, non-resource and processed-goods exports have nearly doubled, reaching their highest level in the period covered by the available figures. This suggests that export growth is increasingly supported not only by traditional commodities but also by goods with greater processing and industrial value.

New markets strengthen

The geography of this growth is particularly notable. China remained Kazakhstan’s largest export market, receiving approximately $7.51 billion, or 18.6% of total exports. Italy followed with $6.98 billion, while Russia, Türkiye, the Netherlands, France and Uzbekistan were also among the leading destinations.

Türkiye stands out as one of the strongest growth markets. Total exports to Türkiye rose by 94.3%, while exports of non-resource and processed goods nearly doubled, from $950 million to $1.91 billion.

The United Kingdom also recorded rapid growth, with exports increasing 2.7 times to $671.8 million.

China remains a key market

Exports of non-resource and processed goods to China increased 12.1% to $3.67 billion. Together, Türkiye, the United Kingdom and China generated roughly $1.8 billion in additional exports compared with the first half of 2025. Uzbekistan, France, Afghanistan and Hong Kong also recorded significant growth.

The broader geography gives Kazakhstan greater access to Asian, European and regional markets and reduces reliance on any single destination.

Industrial goods drive growth

The commodity mix also points to expanding industrial potential. Copper and copper cathodes accounted for $2.84 billion, uranium for $1.51 billion and ferroalloys for $1.1 billion. Exports of copper and copper products increased by nearly 58%, while copper ores and concentrates rose roughly 43%.

The shift toward higher-value exports is also visible in agriculture. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin described Kazakhstan’s oilseed-processing industry as “a successful example of economic diversification,” noting that export revenue from oilseed products had quadrupled to $963 million in four years.

Agricultural products are gaining ground too. Sunflower oil exports reached $533 million, while animal feed products accounted for $438 million in January-June.

Metals, processed products and agricultural goods are gaining importance alongside established resource exports.

The next challenge: moving up the value chain

The next challenge is to turn export growth into lasting gains in higher-value products. This will depend on investment in processing, logistics, infrastructure and market access.

The key question is whether Kazakhstan can sustain growth in processed exports and expand into new markets. The first half of this year points to a shift toward more diverse and higher-value exports with a wider global reach.

World.title: What to Expect from Kurultai Elections in Kazakhstan This Week
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s citizens will elect the members of the Kurultai, a new unicameral Parliament, on Aug. 23, putting a redesigned parliamentary and electoral system into practice for the first time.

Beyond determining who receives the 145 seats, the vote will offer an early indication of how the new rules affect party competition, political representation and the composition of the legislature.

Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework took effect on July 1, replacing the former bicameral Parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis (lower house) and Senate (upper house), with a 145-member Kurultai elected for five years through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to enter the legislature.

Seven political parties are contesting the election, with 545 candidates registered for the race. According to the Central Election Commission (CEC), women, young people and persons with disabilities account for a combined 43.9% of registered candidates, exceeding the 30% cumulative quota required for these groups on party lists.

First test of a new parliamentary model

One of the changes is the disappearance of single-member constituencies from national parliamentary elections.

Under the previous system, legislation passed through the Mazhilis before moving to the Senate. Under the new model, the Kurultai concentrates legislative consideration, and adopted laws are then sent to the President.

Standing committees will take on a larger role in the process. The Kurultai can establish up to eight permanent committees to conduct preliminary reviews of legislation and other parliamentary work. The new framework also formally defines the parliamentary majority and opposition, with opposition representatives guaranteed certain roles in committee leadership, parliamentary hearings and government question sessions.

The election will also mark a transition for the executive branch. After the new Kurultai is elected, the government must formally submit its resignation. The President then has 10 days to decide whether to accept it.

Speaking to The Astana Times, Rassul Kospanov, a senior researcher at the Center for Regional Analysis at the National Analytical Center, said concentrating legislative authority in one chamber could also increase the prominence of its chairperson.

“I think the role of the speaker will become stronger. Previously, the highest legislative authority was divided between two chambers, and that influence was also divided between two speakers; now, in effect, there will be one much more powerful speaker. Much will depend on who takes the position and whether that person can become a trusted and prominent figure for the public,” he said.

Parties face a different electoral test

The electoral system has changed just as significantly. In the previous Mazhilis, 69 of 98 deputies were elected through party lists and 29 through single-member constituencies. All 145 Kurultai members will now be elected through closed party lists in one nationwide constituency, meaning voters choose a party rather than individual candidates within its list.

The 2023 Mazhilis election provides the most recent benchmark. Six parties crossed the 5% threshold, with Amanat, then ruling party that later merged with Adilet, receiving 53.9% of the party-list vote and securing 40 proportional seats. It also won 22 of the 29 single-member constituencies, giving it 62 of the chamber’s 98 seats overall.

That comparison is limited, however, because the system and the party field have both changed. Single-member constituencies have been abolished at the national level, while Amanat has since merged with the Adilet Party.

Kospanov highlighted one direct consequence of removing constituency races: citizens who are not affiliated with political parties no longer have an independent route to the national legislature.

“With the transition to a single nationwide constituency, it is no longer possible to become a member of Parliament if you are not affiliated with a party. There are ordinary citizens and politically active people who do not see a political party they are prepared to join, but under the previous system they still had the right to run. That channel is now completely closed to them,” he said.

He noted, however, that the distinction was less clear in practice, as many deputies elected from single-member constituencies also had political party affiliations.

Kamila Amurtayeva, an expert consultant at the Center for Institutional Analysis and Reforms at the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development (KIPD), told The Astana Times that the fully proportional system both strengthens political parties and raises the demands placed on them.

“There is a paradox here that both strengthens parties and makes their task more difficult,” she said.

“Formally, their role increases sharply because the entire Kurultai is now formed through them, but at the same time they can no longer compensate for a weak party brand with the popularity of individual single-member candidates. Parties will now have to explain to voters not only who represents them, but why voters need that particular party,” she explained.

According to Amurtayeva, the election can therefore serve as a “stress test” for the party system, showing whether parties have stable electoral constituencies and sufficiently distinct political identities.

Seven parties compete for Kurultai seats

Those distinctions have become more visible over nearly four weeks of campaigning. The Astana Times has followed the race through weekly reviews, from the parties’ initial policy pitches and regional campaigning to the first televised debate, an education-focused debate, and the final campaign week’s focus on the rule of law.

Adilet has campaigned on jobs, housing, infrastructure, healthcare and governance. Aq Jol and Respublica have emphasized entrepreneurship, domestic production and economic reform, with the two competing more directly for business-oriented and economically liberal voters. Auyl has remained focused on agriculture and rural communities, while Baytaq has centered its campaign on environmental protection and sustainable development. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) and the People’s Party of Kazakhstan have placed greater emphasis on social policy, labor rights, healthcare and social protection.

Under the new electoral model, those distinctions matter more because every parliamentary seat depends on a party’s nationwide result. The election will therefore provide a clearer measure of which parties have built support around their platforms rather than individual constituency candidates.

Who enters the first Kurultai

The result will also be measured by who ultimately takes the 145 seats.

The 43.9% share of women, young people and persons with disabilities among registered candidates is higher than the statutory 30% cumulative quota. The quota also applies when parties distribute the mandates they win, making the final composition of the Kurultai an important measure of how representation changes under the new system.

Amurtayeva emphasized that the composition of the party factions will therefore matter alongside vote shares and seat totals.

“I would also look at whom the parties actually bring into the Kurultai. Under a fully proportional system, a party has much greater influence over the formation of the deputy corps and therefore bears greater responsibility for its quality. The important indicator will not simply be the percentage of votes or number of seats, but whether the lists renew representation, bring in new professional and social groups, and provide broad regional representation,” she explained.

Kospanov expects some personnel renewal but emphasized that new names should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of an immediate transformation of the political system.

“The renewal will probably be more personal than political, because we are primarily talking about new personnel and new faces. At the same time, many of those described as new faces have simply not served in the Mazhilis or Senate before. A significant number have experience in local maslikhats [local legislative bodies]. For that reason, I would not expect major systemic changes immediately after the election,” he said.

What to watch on Aug. 23

The immediate result will answer several questions about how the new system is taking shape: how many of the seven parties cross the 5% threshold, how the 145 seats are distributed among them and how concentrated or fragmented the first Kurultai becomes.

Turnout will provide another measure of electoral participation, though Amurtayeva highlighted that it should not be treated on its own as an indicator of the quality of political representation.

“High turnout is important for the legitimacy of an election, but by itself it does not tell us about the quality of political representation. The intrigue, in my view, is no longer only whether the voter comes to the polling station, but what the voter does with that vote. These elections are becoming a kind of stress test for the party system itself,” she said.

International observers will provide a separate assessment of how the new electoral framework operates in practice. In an Aug. 13 statement, the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly announced that nearly 80 parliamentarians and staff from around 30 countries would deploy for the election, working with the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and a delegation from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. Their preliminary findings are expected to be presented in Astana on Aug. 24.

Gábor Hajdu, the OSCE special coordinator leading the short-term observers, said the mission would examine how the constitutional and electoral changes are implemented. Lucija Tacer Perlin, head of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly delegation, emphasized that the observers would assess the process without drawing conclusions in advance.

“Our task is not to prejudge how Kazakhstan’s new system will perform, but to examine the process carefully and impartially,” she said.

For Amurtayeva, however, the distinction between the election result and the reform’s broader effect is central to what can realistically be expected from Aug. 23.

“We will know the result of the election quite quickly – the numbers and the names of the deputies – but the result of the reform itself will become clear much later. Roughly a year after the election, it should be possible to see what each party has actually brought into the work of the Kurultai: what issues it advances, whose interests it represents and what changes it has been able to achieve,” she said.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Industrial Growth Reveals Diverging Paths for Manufacturing and Mining
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s economy continued to expand in the first seven months of 2026, with investment and manufacturing providing an important source of growth even as mining output declined and exports remained heavily dependent on raw materials.

New data from the Bureau of National Statistics points to a mixed but potentially significant economic pattern. Industrial output reached nearly 40 trillion tenge (US$83.3 billion), while investment in fixed capital rose to 11.5 trillion tenge (US$24.9 billion) and foreign trade turnover reached $71.8 billion in the first half of the year.

Taken together, the figures suggest that Kazakhstan is attracting and directing more capital toward production and infrastructure. However, the structure of exports shows that the country’s external earnings remain strongly concentrated in commodities, particularly crude oil.

Manufacturing offsets decline in mining

Industrial production reached 39.97 trillion tenge (US$83.23 billion) between January and July, increasing by 3% compared with the same period last year. The most important driver was manufacturing. Output in the sector grew by 9% to 18.83 trillion tenge (US$39.2 billion), accounting for 47.1% of Kazakhstan’s total industrial production.

Growth was particularly strong in pharmaceutical production, which increased by 38.5%, followed by fabricated metal products (+35%), chemicals (+26.9%), and machinery, which grew by 22%. Production of rubber and plastic products increased by 18.6%, food production by 13.9%, and other non-metallic mineral products by 9.4%.

At the same time, mining and quarrying declined by 4.4% to 18.42 trillion tenge (US$38.4 billion). Crude oil production fell by 8.9%, while natural gas output declined by 5.5%.

The contrast between the two sectors is important. Kazakhstan’s industrial economy has historically depended heavily on extractive industries, but the latest figures show manufacturing expanding at a time when mining output is falling. Manufacturing also slightly exceeded mining in the value of industrial production during the seven-month period.

This does not mean that Kazakhstan’s economy has moved away from commodities. Instead, it suggests that other parts of the industrial sector are becoming more capable of supporting growth when output in extractive industries weakens.

Growth was also recorded in electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply, which increased by 12.2%, and in water supply, wastewater and waste collection, which rose by 9.5%.

Investment concentrates on industry, infrastructure and construction

Investment in fixed capital reached 11.5 trillion tenge (US$24 billion) between January and July, increasing by 7.7% in comparable prices. Industry received the largest share of investment, accounting for 41.6% of the total. Manufacturing attracted 14.7% of all investment, while mining accounted for 14%.

The composition of spending also shows that investment is focused primarily on physical expansion. Construction and capital repairs of buildings and structures accounted for 62.1% of investment, while 33.6% was directed toward machinery, equipment and transport.

Transport and warehousing received 17% of total investment, followed by real estate operations at 18.6%. Agriculture, forestry and fisheries accounted for 5.7%. The regional distribution, however, was highly uneven. Investment increased by 94.4% in the Ulytau Region, 56.4% in the Zhambyl Region and 37.5% in the Turkistan Region. Growth was also recorded in the Almaty Region (+16.4%), Abai Region (+16.1%), West Kazakhstan (+13.3%), and the Pavlodar Region (+11.9%).

Meanwhile, investment declined by 24.5% in the Zhetysu Region, 14% in Shymkent, 10.4% in the Karagandy Region and 4.5% in the Mangystau Region. Astana accounted for 11.3% of all investment in fixed capital, while Almaty accounted for 10.8%.

Nearly half of all investment came from large and medium-sized enterprises. Companies’ own funds remained the main source of financing, accounting for 67.7%. Budget funds represented 14%, although their volume declined by 32% compared with January-July 2025.

Bank loans financed 5.6% of investment, while other borrowed funds accounted for 12.7%, including 3% from non-residents.

This financing structure suggests that the current investment cycle is being driven primarily by corporate resources rather than direct state spending or foreign borrowing.
