"It's got to a point where it's lost its critical mass and there's a number of factors why that's happened … and that sugar mill will have to close."

Rocky Point canefarmers were given notice in June. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Race to find another mill

Rather than abandon the industry, Rocky Point growers are now looking for ways to keep growing cane once their local mill stops crushing.

A working group involving canegrowers and other industry stakeholders is investigating whether cane could be transported to Condong Sugar Mill in northern New South Wales, about 100 kilometres away.

"We've actually engaged some trailer manufacturers to potentially look at the most efficient way that we can cart the highest possible payload that we can to New South Wales," Mr Zipf said.

"But look, we're not going to lie down and throw our hands in the air and say, 'We're done.' We're going to be proactive about it and see if we can come up with a resolution."

Owen Menkens, chairman of Canegrowers, said the organisation was working with affected growers to explore their options.

"Sugarcane is a big employer in both the milling sector and in the growing sector," Mr Menkens said.

"It keeps a lot of people employed in a lot of different ways and I think it'll definitely have an effect on the Gold Coast community.

"It's obviously distressing, this period, but I have faith in the growers to be able to come up with a solution."

Prime real estate

The uncertainty surrounding the mill comes at a critical time for the wider Rocky Point region.

The cane growing area is sandwiched between the Gold Coast and Logan and is one of the last major areas of undeveloped land south of Brisbane.

The Rocky Point cane growing region is one of the Gold Coast's last undeveloped sites. (ABC News)

Developers have expressed interest in buying the cane fields in previous decades as the sugar industry has become less viable.

Gold Coast deputy mayor and area councillor Mark Hammel said planning for the future of the district was now a priority.

"The commercial realities facing both the mill and the industry are well understood," Cr Hammel said.

"While we all hope to see the strongest possible outcome for growers, we also have a responsibility to prepare for what comes next.

"Our focus is on ensuring any transition is managed in a way that gives farming families certainty, protects their livelihoods wherever possible, and preserves the region's rich agricultural heritage."

World.title: ‘Grooming’ allegation sparks tense exchange in Alan Jones trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former staffer to Alan Jones who alleges the broadcaster indecently assaulted him as a young man has hit back at suggestions in court that only young children can be groomed by would-be abusers. Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching relating to six male complainants between 2003 and 2020. He vehemently denies the allegations. Alan Jones arriving at court on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Complainant “C”, the second man to give evidence in the trial in Sydney’s Downing Centre Local Court, has alleged Jones kissed him and touched him on the penis without his consent when he worked as a staffer to the broadcaster almost 20 years ago.



At the time of the alleged assaults, which span a five-month period, “C” was aged in his early 20s. During cross-examination on Thursday, Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, showed “C” a message he sent Jones after the former talkback host announced his retirement from 2GB, which was signed off with “love always xo”. The text was sent many years after the alleged assaults. In the message, “C” wrote: “You have only ever treated me with great decency and tremendous generosity. Your kindness towards me has never, ever wavered.” Asked by Bashir if he could have merely said “congratulations”, “C” said he was groomed to write in that manner.



“Well, grooming is something that happens to young children,” Bashir said. “C” responded: “I believe grooming is secretive behaviour that makes you feel you need to behave in a certain way, and you are taught to act in a certain way. “That used to happen, because he used to touch me on the penis.” After “C” agreed he was in his 30s in 2020, more than a decade after the alleged indecent assaults, Bashir suggested Jones never groomed him. “I disagree,” “C” said.



“I was a young man. He was 40 to 45 years older than me, and I was a junior staffer … I still felt that level of power in 2020 because he still was remaining in the media.” Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial exposes rift between former Sydney talkback giants Bashir repeated the assertion that there was no reason for him to say more than “congratulations”. The man said he felt that was how he needed to write it to him at the time, but wished he didn’t. Earlier on Thursday, “C” rejected suggestions his allegations against the former broadcaster stood to benefit Jones’ then-colleague Ray Hadley.



“C” has testified that he confided in Hadley in 2019 that Jones indecently assaulted him more than a decade earlier. Bashir put to “C” that Hadley “was in a position to benefit from any publication” of indecent assault allegations against Jones. “C” said he did not agree. Bashir suggested Hadley and Jones were breakfast radio rivals on 2GB, a characterisation rejected by “C”. “[Jones] just re-signed. That had nothing to do with it,” he said. Complainant “C” denied that he had rehearsed a story in recent years about Jones allegedly indecently assaulting him. “You don’t have to rehearse the truth,” he said. The trial continues.

World.title: ‘Embarrassing backdown’: Labor’s last-minute reprieve for 800,000 Australians
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAged care ‘Embarrassing backdown’: Labor’s last-minute reprieve for 800,000 Australians Brittany Busch August 20, 2026 — 4:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 800,000 older Australians will still get Meals on Wheels and other programs at home after Labor abandoned a plan to merge them into its under-pressure aged care system. Health Minister Mark Butler announced a reprieve on Thursday for the Commonwealth Home Support Program (CHSP), the future of which had been in doubt as the government sought to fold it into its overhaul of the Support at Home program. Health Minister Mark Butler. Dominic Lorrimer The Greens and Coalition were scathing of the government’s delay in backing down from the merger after a parliamentary inquiry recommended in June that the program be kept as a standalone until at least 2030. Labor has now guaranteed funding for the program until at least mid-2029.



It is the third time Labor has made concessions to an unlikely alliance between the Greens and Coalition over its reforms to the ballooning $40 billion aged care budget, after non-government senators forced the government to provide more human oversight of the algorithmic assessments of client’s needs and got the department to fast-track 20,000 home care packages. Related Article Aged care Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate Butler said he had been sceptical for a while about the proposed merger, which Labor inherited from the Morrison government. “[The two programs] deliver quite different services, drawing on quite different capabilities in the communities, and serving quite distinct needs on the part of older Australians,” he said. He praised the work done by “terrific organisations like Meals on Wheels”, which had been delivering food to the elderly since the 1950s, and said he had been worried any changes had to potential to “undermine a lot of the social capital”.



Meals on Wheels Australia chair Paul Sadler said the move had saved the charity from closing services, jeopardising the work of more than 35,000 volunteers nationally. Related Article Aged care Labor’s reforms harm the people they’re supposed to help: aged care watchdog The home support program funds entry-level services to help older Australians maintain their independence, including gardening, cleaning, transport, and food delivery services. It is distinct from Labor’s Support at Home service, which offers clinical in-home care and has been plagued with challenges since its rollout began late last year. Greens spokeswoman for older people Penny Allman-Payne, who chaired the parliamentary inquiry, said the government’s delay had left “older people and providers in the lurch” and some had even left the system.



“Labor’s plan to collapse [CHSP] into its struggling Support at Home program was reckless and dangerous, as the Greens inquiry showed,” the senator said. Opposition aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston said it was an “embarrassing, overdue backdown” from Labor. “Let’s be clear, this was not a proactive decision from a government with a clear plan. Labor has left this decision until the last minute, just as they have done repeatedly throughout their chaotic aged care reforms,” Ruston said in a statement. Chief executive of the Older Persons Advocacy Network, Craig Gear, welcomed the decision, saying more time was needed to consult on and develop reform to the program. World.title: There’s change at the top at Collingwood, as Kelly confirms exit
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 There’s change at the top at Collingwood, as Kelly confirms exit Michael Gleeson August 20, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly will leave the job at the end of next year and take a step back from some of his duties over the next twelve months with the club promoting executive Kerrie Brewer to be the club’s clear second in charge. Kelly said he intends to remain at the club beyond 2027 in a consulting capacity in collaboration with the board. Kerrie Brewer will be promoted to chief operating officer at Collingwood, the second in charge to CEO Craig Kelly. The club has acknowledged there has been a need for a clear 2IC for some time. “I am the CEO of the Collingwood Football Club and I will continue to be so for the next 12 months and from that point will work with the board on projects,” Kelly told this masthead.



“There is a CEO in the building and I am it. What we do need to do is have a chief operating officer and put someone in who understands the club and the AFL. Kerrie Brewer is an outstanding person. She worked here, she went to North Melbourne, went to Hawthorn and helped set up Dingley and I brought her back here from Hawthorn. “She is an outstanding executive. Stepping her up allows me to focus on big projects, liaising with government, the renegotiation with Foxy [Melbourne Cricket Club chief executive Stuart Fox] over the MCG, the Melbourne Olympic Park Trust, the Yarra Council and Victoria Park.” Scott Pendlebury with Magpies president Barry Carp and CEO Craig Kelly. AFL Photos Brewer is highly rated in the industry. She was sponsorship manager at Collingwood for eight years at the start of the 2000s, went to North in a similar role, worked at James Hird’s Gemba marketing company, then moved to Hawthorn for 10 years, moving up to the role of general manager of development infrastructure and government relations. She returned to Collingwood three years ago at executive level, covering similar areas of government relations and infrastructure. Collingwood’s contract to operate at its current home on the Yarra at the old Olympic Park expires in six years. Kelly said the club was eager to invest in the precinct but needed to see the master plan before pursuing further investment and development.



Related Article AFL 2026 Dees to appeal van Rooyen ban; McRae admits having sleepless nights over resting players Tennis Australia has eyed the Collingwood training oval and potentially the Glasshouse facilities for use during the Australian Open, a move Kelly said Collingwood was open to. “We are working with Melbourne Olympic Park Trust now and the government now [about renewing the lease long term] and we have made it very clear we are a crucial part of the environment in the precinct. When you drive by, Collingwood is the hub of activity. “We have launched The Perch temporary facility this week for people to come pre-game and post-game for the next fortnight. We are constantly investing and trying new things for the precinct and our members and fans.” Brewer’s role at Collingwood until this promotion to COO has been to manage these venues, and she is known to have had strong relationships with the key decision-makers at each organisation. She will continue to play a role in managing these venues and contract renewals, but Kelly said day-to-day football issues meant it was important to have a COO to spread the overall workload.



Brewer has not been promoted to the new COO role as part of a formal succession plan into the CEO role when Kelly leaves, but she would be the first among equals in a search next year for Kelly’s replacement. “We have an amazing executive – Susan Harper into Nadine Rabah, Chris Larkins, Lachie McDonald, Charlie Gardiner and Jess Berger – when the time comes and we are looking for a CEO we will go to market externally and internally,” Kelly said. Kelly with head of football Charlie Gardiner. AFL Photos via Getty Images The promotion of Brewer has long been anticipated within the club. It was expected to be announced early this year but was delayed as the club continued to negotiate with Kelly over his future. The club had reportedly also previously sounded out Fremantle chief executive Simon Garlick for his interest in returning to Melbourne as a replacement for Kelly.



In football leadership Collingwood has gone through the season without a head of development, having been unable to find a suitable replacement for Josh Fraser, who left the club at the end of last season to join Carlton. Fraser initially left to join Carlton as their VFL coach but now finds himself having so impressively handled the caretaker tole that he is the permanent senior coach. Fraser had a year to run on his contract at Collingwood as VFL head coach and head of development when he chose instead to leave for Carlton. World.title: Harry wants to go home. Can he return to the royal fold?
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeRoyal family Harry wants to go home. Can he return to the royal fold? Victoria Ward August 20, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: It has been a tumultuous few years for Prince Harry. There have been allegations of racism, neglect and fights over a dog bowl. But now, he’s ready to go home. Harry and Meghan in Melbourne during their visit to Australia in April. Getty Images It has long been known that the Duke of Sussex wanted a refuge in the United Kingdom, a place that would enable him to bring his family over without having to go cap in hand to his father, King Charles, to ask whether there was room at the palace. He wanted the freedom to enjoy British summers, see friends and come and go without the “circus” that has surrounded recent visits – as well as the endless questions about whether he will meet the King, where he might stay and his security.



But what is planned goes far beyond a mere bolthole for flying visits. While nothing is set in stone, the decision to enrol his children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, in a British school suggests the plan is to stay for a long time. Harry with Archie and Lilibet in June. Instagram Whether it will work remains to be seen. Harry and his wife, Meghan, are clearly hedging their bets by keeping their US base in Montecito, despite the vast expense, at least for now. The development marks a significant shift in the Sussexes’ private and professional lives and will have a notable impact on their relationship with the wider royal institution.



The King was only informed of the news on Sunday, and it was not discussed with him during his reunion with the Sussexes at Highgrove last month. Related Article Royal family Harry, Meghan and children to move back to UK He is said to be “naturally pleased” to be able to spend more time with his younger son and his family. However, he remains adamant that the move will not change the couple’s status as private individuals and non-working royals. Until now, the major stumbling block to their coming back has been the family’s security. The duke’s efforts to have his right to guaranteed taxpayer-funded police protection reinstated have been stymied at every turn, in the High Court, in the Court of Appeal and by the Home Office committee responsible for such decisions.



He has insisted it remains too dangerous to bring his wife and children back to the UK without it – a stance that threw the family’s recent travel plans into chaos, prompting Meghan to pull out of two public engagements and be spirited into the country privately with their children for that all-important reunion with the King. It is ultimately up to the British state, through its royal and VIP executive committee, to decide who gets police protection. Harry has had a rift with his brother Prince William, with reports they no longer speak. AP So far, the committee has insisted that the duke and his family must give 30 days’ notice of UK visits so each can be assessed on its merits, a “bespoke” arrangement through which they have largely been denied protection. There is no detail on any new plan. What has prompted this apparent about-face and how would it work?



A potential move out of the US has been on the cards for some time. The Sussexes bought a luxury villa in Portugal in 2023. They are said to have paid £6.3 million ($12 million) for the property, in the wealthy enclave of Costa Terra, a private golf and leisure resort in Melides, a little over 100 kilometres south of Lisbon. It happens to count Jack Brooksbank, husband of Harry’s cousin Princess Eugenie, among its employees. Jack and Eugenie also have a home there, where they spend much of the year. Harry and Meghan with Archie and Lilibet on holidays in Portugal this year. Instagram The duke and duchess spent a couple of weeks on holiday in Portugal recently, ahead of their visit to the UK, and are keen to return more often. Portugal is also friendly towards US citizens who want to make the country their home, with a generous “golden visa” program for wealthy immigrants that allows easy access to all of the EU.



The duke has made no secret of his desire for his children to experience life in the UK – to understand their British heritage, and the country’s culture and customs, beyond simply pronouncing zebra in the English way. On a more personal level, he simply wants them to enjoy a relationship with his own family, his maternal aunts and uncle with whom he remains close, and hopefully, his father. Then-prince Charles with William and Harry in France in 2017. Philippe Huguen/AP When they moved abroad, the duke and duchess were told in no uncertain terms that the “half in, half out” approach they wanted to adopt was out of the question. The late Queen was adamant, saying they could not promote charitable endeavours on behalf of the Crown while pursuing commercial interests.



Over in the US, the couple became involved with a handful of grassroots organisations, but Archewell, their philanthropic vehicle, has faded into the shadows. The duke tried to get on board with the showbiz lark. Yes, there was money to be made, but his heart was never in it. The Netflix deals, Spotify, podcasts … they were never really his thing. Harry has long wanted to give more time and energy to his UK charities, while Meghan continues to be busy with As Ever, her lifestyle business. He loves being in the UK. He loves spending time with the Invictus community, as well as the children of Scotty’s Little Soldiers and WellChild.



Last year, he donated £1 million to Children in Need and pledged his continued support for youth charities in Nottingham. The couple believe they have proved they can make an independent living while still supporting their charitable causes. Meghan and Harry at Bondi Beach in April. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP A successful visit to Australia in April was held up as an example of this model in action. Their charitable endeavours remain independent, as opposed to so-called “representative duties” on behalf of the institution. Why come back now? The American dream is perhaps not all it’s cracked up to be in Donald Trump’s US. It is no secret that the couple’s politics do not align with the president’s.



The duke and duchess enjoy their freedom in the Californian sunshine, the walks on the beach, swimming in the sea, surfing and the space to move around with relative freedom. But for the duke, at least, it is a long way from home. Harry and Meghan’s California home. Meghan, who has always made a virtue of being entwined with her “love”, appears to be taking one for the team. What are her own motivations to return to a country that holds less than happy memories? Only time will tell.



The lure of her favoured radio station, Magic FM, and her affection for the quaint British tradition of Christmas crackers are unlikely to be enough. Related Article Updated

Royal family King and Queen meet with Prince Harry, Meghan and children The duchess has been scathing about much of her time within the royal fold, which she revealed in 2021 had pushed her to contemplate suicide. She also struggled to get to grips with certain elements of British life, such as the “stiff upper lip”. She once suggested that she would never be able to do the school run in the UK without it turning into a media frenzy. Harry, though, is convinced that the negative narrative is at odds with how his wife is perceived.



The couple are, for now, keeping the location of their new UK base private. Their last British home was Frogmore Cottage on the Windsor estate, which was given to them as a wedding present by Elizabeth II in May 2018. Harry and Meghan – with her mother Doria Ragland – show their newborn son to Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip at Windsor Castle in 2019. AP However, they were evicted in early summer 2023, rendering them “homeless” when on UK soil. Harry has been offered accommodation at Buckingham Palace more than once but has turned it down over security concerns.



Last month’s debacle over accommodation proved the last straw. The duke had been forced to request access to an apartment on one of the royal estates, or otherwise stay with friends or at a hotel. Related Article Princess Diana Princess Diana’s brother writes new book about her, vowing to correct ‘untruths’ The couple had previously rented a four-bed farmhouse on the Great Tew Estate in the Oxfordshire Cotswolds. It was used as a rural escape from Nottingham Cottage, the Kensington Palace property where Harry lived when the couple first met. They had to give up the country bolthole when paparazzi took aerial shots of it in January 2019. On the couple’s most recent visit last month, they stayed with Earl Spencer, the duke’s uncle, on his Althorp estate in Northamptonshire.



While the duke has remained close to the Spencers, his late mother’s side of the family, he has made no secret of his desire to reconcile with the other side. He admitted in 2023 that he hoped he would one day be “joined at the hip” with Prince William again. Meghan and Harry watching basketball in California in February. Getty Images But he suggested there needed to be “conversations in order for reconciliation”, which had to involve his family taking their share of accountability. The Prince and Princess of Wales long ago cut off contact with the Sussexes, feeling deeply betrayed by the private family revelations and allegations aired in public.



Last May, the duke told the BBC that he would “love” a reconciliation with his family. “There’s no point in continuing to fight,” he said, acknowledging that, while he could “forgive” his father, brother and stepmother for the many disagreements of the past, “some members of the royal family” would never forgive him for writing a memoir, or for “lots of things”. Loading His father’s cancer diagnosis, unsurprisingly, appears to have been a wake-up call. His relationship with the King is perhaps much warmer than many realise.



With the legal battle over security in the past, the pair are regularly in touch, and the duke is delighted that his father has shown an interest in his life abroad. Related Article Updated

Royal family Prince Harry claims William physically attacked him, hints at not attending Charles III’s coronation His relationship with his stepmother, Camilla, is a different story entirely, and he has made no secret of his feelings. He has described the Queen as “the villain” in his parents’ marriage, whose need to rehabilitate her image made her “dangerous” because of her connections within the British press. Harry has wrestled with all of these feelings since moving abroad.



There can be no doubt that the pull of the UK has been strong. Last year, he said he had always loved his country and missed “parts of the UK” and admitted that the thought he would not be able to show his children his “homeland” had brought him much sadness. The Sussexes’ imminent relocation will at least begin to reverse that tide. The Telegraph, London Read more of our royal coverage here:

World.title: Did CBA boss Matt Comyn’s marriage breakdown meet the public interest test?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMatt Comyn Opinion Did CBA boss Matt Comyn’s marriage breakdown meet the public interest test? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 20, 2026 — 3:45pm

August 20, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When investment firm Magellan’s co-founder and major shareholder Hamish Douglass separated from his wife in 2021, the media’s publication of the news was considered controversial. It was justified, in part, because it might result in the sale of a swathe of his shareholding and control of the company could change. Douglass was never a household name outside the business community, but inside the finance goldfish bowl he was a public figure and the impact any large share sale would have on other Magellan investors was significant. Commonwealth Bank chief Matt Comyn presents the bank’s full year 2026 results earlier this month. Nic Long He was the talisman for his company, and many of its clients had been in his thrall. In the world of funds management, Douglass was a celebrity. Fast-forward to this week’s news that Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn is separating from his wife of a couple of decades – an event which raises the question whether, or at what point, does any executive’s private life become fair game.



From the outset that justification for disclosing Douglass’ marital status does not apply to Comyn. His stake in CBA is worth serious money to most people, inconsequential in the scheme of the $262 billion company, and the sale of any or all of his stake won’t move the dial. But shareholders definitely want to see the most senior executive of their company with a certain degree of share ownership, so Comyn’s recent sale of $8.4 million in shares can now be understood as likely part of dealing with his personal affairs amid the separation. Without this extra piece of personal information, CBA shareholders could become concerned that Comyn was cashing out stock and sending a signal that shares were overvalued. (There is a reason for the ASX rules that dictate executives and directors of listed companies have to disclose any share sales). Another argument in favour of disclosure of personal information says that shareholders have a legitimate right to know of issues that may be distracting to the chief executive’s exercise of his duties.



(That said, the outwardly unflappable Comyn has not missed a management beat – at least not publicly. Last week he delivered a strong 2026 year profit, seemingly without raising a sweat.) The above reasoning pushes Comyn’s private news at least some ways towards passing the public interest test. But more broadly, in this modern digital information age, Comyn is a public figure. From regular grabs on national television, to his carefully curated opinions featured in every news publication, to podcasts about what he eats for breakfast and even his exercise regime, Comyn has curated a public profile. Part of his highly remunerated job is being the public face of CBA – the country’s largest company. And his success in leading the bank, which has 800,000 investors, 16 million customers and 55,000 staff has landed him as a de facto proxy for big business in Australia.



His close relationship with the Albanese government and Treasurer Jim Chalmers in particular has also recognisably boosted his influence on public policy. Related Article Opinion

CBD Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn enters his bachelor era John Buckley CBD columnist My fellow journalist and author of this week’s scoop, John Buckley, says there is a kind of “cult of Comyn” that extends beyond the business community. Of course there will be a cohort of readers and Comyn supporters that understandably consider the publication of details of his personal life inappropriate or even voyeuristic. Do they also consider the details of James Packer’s relationships to be off limits? Do they snigger each time Rupert Murdoch lands yet another wife, even in his 90s?



Mike Cannon-Brookes or Andrew Forrest or even Keir Nielson (founder of Platinum Asset Management), had publicised marital breakdowns, all of which were reported. Of course, they all had shareholdings large enough to, at least potentially, cause major changes for their companies, depending on how their separations played out. I am sure none of them enjoyed their laundry being aired in public even if there was nothing particularly controversial about the breakdown in their marriage. It is an unfortunate fact of life that being the public face of a major institution like the Commonwealth Bank has made Comyn a public figure and the closest thing Australia has got to a business celebrity. World.title: Hannah McGuire’s killer found not guilty of raping student two months before murder
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCourts Hannah McGuire’s killer found not guilty of raping student two months before murder Erin Pearson August 20, 2026 — 3:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The killer of young Ballarat woman Hannah McGuire has been found not guilty of raping a 16-year-old student two months before the murder. It can now be revealed, after a suppression order was lifted, that Lachlan Young, 24, had been accused of forcing a girl he’d just met to have sex with him in a neighbour’s backyard during a party. A courtroom sketch of Lachlan Young during his rape trial. Anita Lester Weeks after the alleged rape, Young attacked and killed his ex-girlfriend, McGuire, 23, burnt her body in a car in a state forest and tried to make her death look like suicide. On Thursday, a County Court jury of 10 men and two women found Young not guilty of rape following two days of deliberations. It followed a week-long trial, which took place without the jury hearing of Young’s criminal background.



The jury was told that in February 2024, the alleged victim and a group of friends spent the day together, ate at a Ballarat hotel and then attended a home in the Ballarat suburb of Sebastopol. Prosecutor Andrew Buckland told the court that while the group was at the house, an older sibling arrived with his friend, Young, to socialise in the shed. There, the larger group played pool, drank alcohol and sat by the fire. Hannah McGuire, 23, was murdered in her home in 2024 by her ex-partner, Lachlan Young. When some of the younger members of the group went to bed, Young had sat beside the complainant and asked for her Snapchat. Buckland said Young was then accused of asking if she “wanted to do something” but the girl refused and went to bed.



The pair allegedly continued to exchange messages, including the girl writing to Young: “do you know how old I am”, and “no, I’m 16″. The girl told the jury that about 3am, she agreed to meet Young in the backyard where she consented to him putting his hands into her shorts. He then allegedly asked, “Do you want to f---?” The girl told the court she said no, but accused Young of forcing himself onto her. The next day, the jury heard, the girl told one of her friends she was raped by Young. The trial heard that weeks later, she messaged Young to say, “how’s ya missus? How would she feel about f---ing an underage and cheating on her?” and later “you’re pathetic Lachie, you f---ed me even though I said no”.



Young blocked the girl, and she later reported the alleged rape to a school wellbeing counsellor who contacted police. Young (centre) is already serving a jail term of at least 22 years for murdering McGuire. Instagram During the trial, Young gave evidence and denied raping the teenage complainant. He told the jury that during the evening in February 2024 he had communicated “very little” with the girl over Snapchat, believing she was over 18. “She was there drinking alcohol and I overheard a conversation that they had been at the pub earlier that night,” he said.



Young said that about 6am the next day, he left the shed and the complainant came out to meet him. “One thing’s led to another and we’ve come on to each other. We started kissing,” Young told the court. The carpenter said that during this time, the girl told him she was 16 and he said he gently pushed her away. “I wasn’t interested in the age gap and I didn’t wanna go down that path of getting into trouble. I said, ‘Nothing more can happen’, and, ‘Sorry, but I’m not interested’,” Young told the jury. “Once I said that, I started to walk back to the shed and she’s sort of followed me and she said that it’s fine and no one will have to know and no one will get in any trouble. I said, ‘Sorry, I’m still not interested’, and I continued to walk back to the shed.”



Related Article Updated

Courts ‘I will never forgive,’ Hannah McGuire’s mother tells her daughter’s murderer Young maintained he and the girl were in the backyard together for about five minutes. He told the trial he later blocked her on Snapchat because he didn’t want to entertain claims he raped her. While under cross-examination, Young said: “I had a partner at home. I was doing the wrong thing and it shouldn’t have got to that stage and I pulled it up.” Young is already serving a jail term of 28 years, with a non-parole period of 22 years and four months, for what a judge last year described as the “brutal and callous” murder of McGuire, which was “extreme act of domestic violence”. Young strangled his ex-girlfriend on the bathroom floor of the home they once shared in Sebastopol, in Ballarat’s south, about 2.30am on April 5, 2024.

World.title: ‘Grooming’ allegation sparks tense exchange in Alan Jones trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former staffer to Alan Jones who alleges the broadcaster indecently assaulted him as a young man has hit back at suggestions in court that only young children can be groomed by would-be abusers. Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching relating to six male complainants between 2003 and 2020. He vehemently denies the allegations. Alan Jones arriving at court on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Complainant “C”, the second man to give evidence in the trial in Sydney’s Downing Centre Local Court, has alleged Jones kissed him and touched him on the penis without his consent when he worked as a staffer to the broadcaster almost 20 years ago.



At the time of the alleged assaults, which span a five-month period, “C” was aged in his early 20s. During cross-examination on Thursday, Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, showed “C” a message he sent Jones after the former talkback host announced his retirement from 2GB, which was signed off with “love always xo”. The text was sent many years after the alleged assaults. In the message, “C” wrote: “You have only ever treated me with great decency and tremendous generosity. Your kindness towards me has never, ever wavered.” Asked by Bashir if he could have merely said “congratulations”, “C” said he was groomed to write in that manner.



“Well, grooming is something that happens to young children,” Bashir said. “C” responded: “I believe grooming is secretive behaviour that makes you feel you need to behave in a certain way, and you are taught to act in a certain way. “That used to happen, because he used to touch me on the penis.” After “C” agreed he was in his 30s in 2020, more than a decade after the alleged indecent assaults, Bashir suggested Jones never groomed him. “I disagree,” “C” said.



“I was a young man. He was 40 to 45 years older than me, and I was a junior staffer … I still felt that level of power in 2020 because he still was remaining in the media.” Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones trial exposes rift between former Sydney talkback giants Bashir repeated the assertion that there was no reason for him to say more than “congratulations”. The man said he felt that was how he needed to write it to him at the time, but wished he didn’t. Earlier on Thursday, “C” rejected suggestions his allegations against the former broadcaster stood to benefit Jones’ then-colleague Ray Hadley.



“C” has testified that he confided in Hadley in 2019 that Jones indecently assaulted him more than a decade earlier. Bashir put to “C” that Hadley “was in a position to benefit from any publication” of indecent assault allegations against Jones. “C” said he did not agree. Bashir suggested Hadley and Jones were breakfast radio rivals on 2GB, a characterisation rejected by “C”. “[Jones] just re-signed. That had nothing to do with it,” he said. Complainant “C” denied that he had rehearsed a story in recent years about Jones allegedly indecently assaulting him. “You don’t have to rehearse the truth,” he said. The trial continues.

World.title: ‘Embarrassing backdown’: Labor’s last-minute reprieve for 800,000 Australians
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAged care ‘Embarrassing backdown’: Labor’s last-minute reprieve for 800,000 Australians Brittany Busch August 20, 2026 — 4:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 800,000 older Australians will still get Meals on Wheels and other programs at home after Labor abandoned a plan to merge them into its under-pressure aged care system. Health Minister Mark Butler announced a reprieve on Thursday for the Commonwealth Home Support Program (CHSP), the future of which had been in doubt as the government sought to fold it into its overhaul of the Support at Home program. Health Minister Mark Butler. Dominic Lorrimer The Greens and Coalition were scathing of the government’s delay in backing down from the merger after a parliamentary inquiry recommended in June that the program be kept as a standalone until at least 2030. Labor has now guaranteed funding for the program until at least mid-2029.



It is the third time Labor has made concessions to an unlikely alliance between the Greens and Coalition over its reforms to the ballooning $40 billion aged care budget, after non-government senators forced the government to provide more human oversight of the algorithmic assessments of client’s needs and got the department to fast-track 20,000 home care packages. Related Article Aged care Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate Butler said he had been sceptical for a while about the proposed merger, which Labor inherited from the Morrison government. “[The two programs] deliver quite different services, drawing on quite different capabilities in the communities, and serving quite distinct needs on the part of older Australians,” he said. He praised the work done by “terrific organisations like Meals on Wheels”, which had been delivering food to the elderly since the 1950s, and said he had been worried any changes had to potential to “undermine a lot of the social capital”.



Meals on Wheels Australia chair Paul Sadler said the move had saved the charity from closing services, jeopardising the work of more than 35,000 volunteers nationally. Related Article Aged care Labor’s reforms harm the people they’re supposed to help: aged care watchdog The home support program funds entry-level services to help older Australians maintain their independence, including gardening, cleaning, transport, and food delivery services. It is distinct from Labor’s Support at Home service, which offers clinical in-home care and has been plagued with challenges since its rollout began late last year. Greens spokeswoman for older people Penny Allman-Payne, who chaired the parliamentary inquiry, said the government’s delay had left “older people and providers in the lurch” and some had even left the system.



“Labor’s plan to collapse [CHSP] into its struggling Support at Home program was reckless and dangerous, as the Greens inquiry showed,” the senator said. Opposition aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston said it was an “embarrassing, overdue backdown” from Labor. “Let’s be clear, this was not a proactive decision from a government with a clear plan. Labor has left this decision until the last minute, just as they have done repeatedly throughout their chaotic aged care reforms,” Ruston said in a statement. Chief executive of the Older Persons Advocacy Network, Craig Gear, welcomed the decision, saying more time was needed to consult on and develop reform to the program. World.title: There’s change at the top at Collingwood, as Kelly confirms exit
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 There’s change at the top at Collingwood, as Kelly confirms exit Michael Gleeson August 20, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly will leave the job at the end of next year and take a step back from some of his duties over the next twelve months with the club promoting executive Kerrie Brewer to be the club’s clear second in charge. Kelly said he intends to remain at the club beyond 2027 in a consulting capacity in collaboration with the board. Kerrie Brewer will be promoted to chief operating officer at Collingwood, the second in charge to CEO Craig Kelly. The club has acknowledged there has been a need for a clear 2IC for some time. “I am the CEO of the Collingwood Football Club and I will continue to be so for the next 12 months and from that point will work with the board on projects,” Kelly told this masthead.



“There is a CEO in the building and I am it. What we do need to do is have a chief operating officer and put someone in who understands the club and the AFL. Kerrie Brewer is an outstanding person. She worked here, she went to North Melbourne, went to Hawthorn and helped set up Dingley and I brought her back here from Hawthorn. “She is an outstanding executive. Stepping her up allows me to focus on big projects, liaising with government, the renegotiation with Foxy [Melbourne Cricket Club chief executive Stuart Fox] over the MCG, the Melbourne Olympic Park Trust, the Yarra Council and Victoria Park.” Scott Pendlebury with Magpies president Barry Carp and CEO Craig Kelly. AFL Photos Brewer is highly rated in the industry. She was sponsorship manager at Collingwood for eight years at the start of the 2000s, went to North in a similar role, worked at James Hird’s Gemba marketing company, then moved to Hawthorn for 10 years, moving up to the role of general manager of development infrastructure and government relations. She returned to Collingwood three years ago at executive level, covering similar areas of government relations and infrastructure. Collingwood’s contract to operate at its current home on the Yarra at the old Olympic Park expires in six years. Kelly said the club was eager to invest in the precinct but needed to see the master plan before pursuing further investment and development.



Related Article AFL 2026 Dees to appeal van Rooyen ban; McRae admits having sleepless nights over resting players Tennis Australia has eyed the Collingwood training oval and potentially the Glasshouse facilities for use during the Australian Open, a move Kelly said Collingwood was open to. “We are working with Melbourne Olympic Park Trust now and the government now [about renewing the lease long term] and we have made it very clear we are a crucial part of the environment in the precinct. When you drive by, Collingwood is the hub of activity. “We have launched The Perch temporary facility this week for people to come pre-game and post-game for the next fortnight. We are constantly investing and trying new things for the precinct and our members and fans.” Brewer’s role at Collingwood until this promotion to COO has been to manage these venues, and she is known to have had strong relationships with the key decision-makers at each organisation. She will continue to play a role in managing these venues and contract renewals, but Kelly said day-to-day football issues meant it was important to have a COO to spread the overall workload.



Brewer has not been promoted to the new COO role as part of a formal succession plan into the CEO role when Kelly leaves, but she would be the first among equals in a search next year for Kelly’s replacement. “We have an amazing executive – Susan Harper into Nadine Rabah, Chris Larkins, Lachie McDonald, Charlie Gardiner and Jess Berger – when the time comes and we are looking for a CEO we will go to market externally and internally,” Kelly said. Kelly with head of football Charlie Gardiner. AFL Photos via Getty Images The promotion of Brewer has long been anticipated within the club. It was expected to be announced early this year but was delayed as the club continued to negotiate with Kelly over his future. The club had reportedly also previously sounded out Fremantle chief executive Simon Garlick for his interest in returning to Melbourne as a replacement for Kelly.



In football leadership Collingwood has gone through the season without a head of development, having been unable to find a suitable replacement for Josh Fraser, who left the club at the end of last season to join Carlton. Fraser initially left to join Carlton as their VFL coach but now finds himself having so impressively handled the caretaker tole that he is the permanent senior coach. Fraser had a year to run on his contract at Collingwood as VFL head coach and head of development when he chose instead to leave for Carlton. World.title: Harry wants to go home. Can he return to the royal fold?
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeRoyal family Harry wants to go home. Can he return to the royal fold? Victoria Ward August 20, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: It has been a tumultuous few years for Prince Harry. There have been allegations of racism, neglect and fights over a dog bowl. But now, he’s ready to go home. Harry and Meghan in Melbourne during their visit to Australia in April. Getty Images It has long been known that the Duke of Sussex wanted a refuge in the United Kingdom, a place that would enable him to bring his family over without having to go cap in hand to his father, King Charles, to ask whether there was room at the palace. He wanted the freedom to enjoy British summers, see friends and come and go without the “circus” that has surrounded recent visits – as well as the endless questions about whether he will meet the King, where he might stay and his security.



But what is planned goes far beyond a mere bolthole for flying visits. While nothing is set in stone, the decision to enrol his children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, in a British school suggests the plan is to stay for a long time. Harry with Archie and Lilibet in June. Instagram Whether it will work remains to be seen. Harry and his wife, Meghan, are clearly hedging their bets by keeping their US base in Montecito, despite the vast expense, at least for now. The development marks a significant shift in the Sussexes’ private and professional lives and will have a notable impact on their relationship with the wider royal institution.



The King was only informed of the news on Sunday, and it was not discussed with him during his reunion with the Sussexes at Highgrove last month. Related Article Royal family Harry, Meghan and children to move back to UK He is said to be “naturally pleased” to be able to spend more time with his younger son and his family. However, he remains adamant that the move will not change the couple’s status as private individuals and non-working royals. Until now, the major stumbling block to their coming back has been the family’s security. The duke’s efforts to have his right to guaranteed taxpayer-funded police protection reinstated have been stymied at every turn, in the High Court, in the Court of Appeal and by the Home Office committee responsible for such decisions.



He has insisted it remains too dangerous to bring his wife and children back to the UK without it – a stance that threw the family’s recent travel plans into chaos, prompting Meghan to pull out of two public engagements and be spirited into the country privately with their children for that all-important reunion with the King. It is ultimately up to the British state, through its royal and VIP executive committee, to decide who gets police protection. Harry has had a rift with his brother Prince William, with reports they no longer speak. AP So far, the committee has insisted that the duke and his family must give 30 days’ notice of UK visits so each can be assessed on its merits, a “bespoke” arrangement through which they have largely been denied protection. There is no detail on any new plan. What has prompted this apparent about-face and how would it work?



A potential move out of the US has been on the cards for some time. The Sussexes bought a luxury villa in Portugal in 2023. They are said to have paid £6.3 million ($12 million) for the property, in the wealthy enclave of Costa Terra, a private golf and leisure resort in Melides, a little over 100 kilometres south of Lisbon. It happens to count Jack Brooksbank, husband of Harry’s cousin Princess Eugenie, among its employees. Jack and Eugenie also have a home there, where they spend much of the year. Harry and Meghan with Archie and Lilibet on holidays in Portugal this year. Instagram The duke and duchess spent a couple of weeks on holiday in Portugal recently, ahead of their visit to the UK, and are keen to return more often. Portugal is also friendly towards US citizens who want to make the country their home, with a generous “golden visa” program for wealthy immigrants that allows easy access to all of the EU.



The duke has made no secret of his desire for his children to experience life in the UK – to understand their British heritage, and the country’s culture and customs, beyond simply pronouncing zebra in the English way. On a more personal level, he simply wants them to enjoy a relationship with his own family, his maternal aunts and uncle with whom he remains close, and hopefully, his father. Then-prince Charles with William and Harry in France in 2017. Philippe Huguen/AP When they moved abroad, the duke and duchess were told in no uncertain terms that the “half in, half out” approach they wanted to adopt was out of the question. The late Queen was adamant, saying they could not promote charitable endeavours on behalf of the Crown while pursuing commercial interests.



Over in the US, the couple became involved with a handful of grassroots organisations, but Archewell, their philanthropic vehicle, has faded into the shadows. The duke tried to get on board with the showbiz lark. Yes, there was money to be made, but his heart was never in it. The Netflix deals, Spotify, podcasts … they were never really his thing. Harry has long wanted to give more time and energy to his UK charities, while Meghan continues to be busy with As Ever, her lifestyle business. He loves being in the UK. He loves spending time with the Invictus community, as well as the children of Scotty’s Little Soldiers and WellChild.



Last year, he donated £1 million to Children in Need and pledged his continued support for youth charities in Nottingham. The couple believe they have proved they can make an independent living while still supporting their charitable causes. Meghan and Harry at Bondi Beach in April. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP A successful visit to Australia in April was held up as an example of this model in action. Their charitable endeavours remain independent, as opposed to so-called “representative duties” on behalf of the institution. Why come back now? The American dream is perhaps not all it’s cracked up to be in Donald Trump’s US. It is no secret that the couple’s politics do not align with the president’s.



The duke and duchess enjoy their freedom in the Californian sunshine, the walks on the beach, swimming in the sea, surfing and the space to move around with relative freedom. But for the duke, at least, it is a long way from home. Harry and Meghan’s California home. Meghan, who has always made a virtue of being entwined with her “love”, appears to be taking one for the team. What are her own motivations to return to a country that holds less than happy memories? Only time will tell.



The lure of her favoured radio station, Magic FM, and her affection for the quaint British tradition of Christmas crackers are unlikely to be enough. Related Article Updated

Royal family King and Queen meet with Prince Harry, Meghan and children The duchess has been scathing about much of her time within the royal fold, which she revealed in 2021 had pushed her to contemplate suicide. She also struggled to get to grips with certain elements of British life, such as the “stiff upper lip”. She once suggested that she would never be able to do the school run in the UK without it turning into a media frenzy. Harry, though, is convinced that the negative narrative is at odds with how his wife is perceived.



The couple are, for now, keeping the location of their new UK base private. Their last British home was Frogmore Cottage on the Windsor estate, which was given to them as a wedding present by Elizabeth II in May 2018. Harry and Meghan – with her mother Doria Ragland – show their newborn son to Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip at Windsor Castle in 2019. AP However, they were evicted in early summer 2023, rendering them “homeless” when on UK soil. Harry has been offered accommodation at Buckingham Palace more than once but has turned it down over security concerns.



Last month’s debacle over accommodation proved the last straw. The duke had been forced to request access to an apartment on one of the royal estates, or otherwise stay with friends or at a hotel. Related Article Princess Diana Princess Diana’s brother writes new book about her, vowing to correct ‘untruths’ The couple had previously rented a four-bed farmhouse on the Great Tew Estate in the Oxfordshire Cotswolds. It was used as a rural escape from Nottingham Cottage, the Kensington Palace property where Harry lived when the couple first met. They had to give up the country bolthole when paparazzi took aerial shots of it in January 2019. On the couple’s most recent visit last month, they stayed with Earl Spencer, the duke’s uncle, on his Althorp estate in Northamptonshire.



While the duke has remained close to the Spencers, his late mother’s side of the family, he has made no secret of his desire to reconcile with the other side. He admitted in 2023 that he hoped he would one day be “joined at the hip” with Prince William again. Meghan and Harry watching basketball in California in February. Getty Images But he suggested there needed to be “conversations in order for reconciliation”, which had to involve his family taking their share of accountability. The Prince and Princess of Wales long ago cut off contact with the Sussexes, feeling deeply betrayed by the private family revelations and allegations aired in public.



Last May, the duke told the BBC that he would “love” a reconciliation with his family. “There’s no point in continuing to fight,” he said, acknowledging that, while he could “forgive” his father, brother and stepmother for the many disagreements of the past, “some members of the royal family” would never forgive him for writing a memoir, or for “lots of things”. Loading His father’s cancer diagnosis, unsurprisingly, appears to have been a wake-up call. His relationship with the King is perhaps much warmer than many realise.



With the legal battle over security in the past, the pair are regularly in touch, and the duke is delighted that his father has shown an interest in his life abroad. Related Article Updated

Royal family Prince Harry claims William physically attacked him, hints at not attending Charles III’s coronation His relationship with his stepmother, Camilla, is a different story entirely, and he has made no secret of his feelings. He has described the Queen as “the villain” in his parents’ marriage, whose need to rehabilitate her image made her “dangerous” because of her connections within the British press. Harry has wrestled with all of these feelings since moving abroad.



There can be no doubt that the pull of the UK has been strong. Last year, he said he had always loved his country and missed “parts of the UK” and admitted that the thought he would not be able to show his children his “homeland” had brought him much sadness. The Sussexes’ imminent relocation will at least begin to reverse that tide. The Telegraph, London Read more of our royal coverage here:

World.title: Did CBA boss Matt Comyn’s marriage breakdown meet the public interest test?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMatt Comyn Opinion Did CBA boss Matt Comyn’s marriage breakdown meet the public interest test? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 20, 2026 — 3:45pm

August 20, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When investment firm Magellan’s co-founder and major shareholder Hamish Douglass separated from his wife in 2021, the media’s publication of the news was considered controversial. It was justified, in part, because it might result in the sale of a swathe of his shareholding and control of the company could change. Douglass was never a household name outside the business community, but inside the finance goldfish bowl he was a public figure and the impact any large share sale would have on other Magellan investors was significant. Commonwealth Bank chief Matt Comyn presents the bank’s full year 2026 results earlier this month. Nic Long He was the talisman for his company, and many of its clients had been in his thrall. In the world of funds management, Douglass was a celebrity. Fast-forward to this week’s news that Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn is separating from his wife of a couple of decades – an event which raises the question whether, or at what point, does any executive’s private life become fair game.



From the outset that justification for disclosing Douglass’ marital status does not apply to Comyn. His stake in CBA is worth serious money to most people, inconsequential in the scheme of the $262 billion company, and the sale of any or all of his stake won’t move the dial. But shareholders definitely want to see the most senior executive of their company with a certain degree of share ownership, so Comyn’s recent sale of $8.4 million in shares can now be understood as likely part of dealing with his personal affairs amid the separation. Without this extra piece of personal information, CBA shareholders could become concerned that Comyn was cashing out stock and sending a signal that shares were overvalued. (There is a reason for the ASX rules that dictate executives and directors of listed companies have to disclose any share sales). Another argument in favour of disclosure of personal information says that shareholders have a legitimate right to know of issues that may be distracting to the chief executive’s exercise of his duties.



(That said, the outwardly unflappable Comyn has not missed a management beat – at least not publicly. Last week he delivered a strong 2026 year profit, seemingly without raising a sweat.) The above reasoning pushes Comyn’s private news at least some ways towards passing the public interest test. But more broadly, in this modern digital information age, Comyn is a public figure. From regular grabs on national television, to his carefully curated opinions featured in every news publication, to podcasts about what he eats for breakfast and even his exercise regime, Comyn has curated a public profile. Part of his highly remunerated job is being the public face of CBA – the country’s largest company. And his success in leading the bank, which has 800,000 investors, 16 million customers and 55,000 staff has landed him as a de facto proxy for big business in Australia.



His close relationship with the Albanese government and Treasurer Jim Chalmers in particular has also recognisably boosted his influence on public policy. Related Article Opinion

CBD Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn enters his bachelor era John Buckley CBD columnist My fellow journalist and author of this week’s scoop, John Buckley, says there is a kind of “cult of Comyn” that extends beyond the business community. Of course there will be a cohort of readers and Comyn supporters that understandably consider the publication of details of his personal life inappropriate or even voyeuristic. Do they also consider the details of James Packer’s relationships to be off limits? Do they snigger each time Rupert Murdoch lands yet another wife, even in his 90s?



Mike Cannon-Brookes or Andrew Forrest or even Keir Nielson (founder of Platinum Asset Management), had publicised marital breakdowns, all of which were reported. Of course, they all had shareholdings large enough to, at least potentially, cause major changes for their companies, depending on how their separations played out. I am sure none of them enjoyed their laundry being aired in public even if there was nothing particularly controversial about the breakdown in their marriage. It is an unfortunate fact of life that being the public face of a major institution like the Commonwealth Bank has made Comyn a public figure and the closest thing Australia has got to a business celebrity. World.title: Hannah McGuire’s killer found not guilty of raping student two months before murder
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCourts Hannah McGuire’s killer found not guilty of raping student two months before murder Erin Pearson August 20, 2026 — 3:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The killer of young Ballarat woman Hannah McGuire has been found not guilty of raping a 16-year-old student two months before the murder. It can now be revealed, after a suppression order was lifted, that Lachlan Young, 24, had been accused of forcing a girl he’d just met to have sex with him in a neighbour’s backyard during a party. A courtroom sketch of Lachlan Young during his rape trial. Anita Lester Weeks after the alleged rape, Young attacked and killed his ex-girlfriend, McGuire, 23, burnt her body in a car in a state forest and tried to make her death look like suicide. On Thursday, a County Court jury of 10 men and two women found Young not guilty of rape following two days of deliberations. It followed a week-long trial, which took place without the jury hearing of Young’s criminal background.



The jury was told that in February 2024, the alleged victim and a group of friends spent the day together, ate at a Ballarat hotel and then attended a home in the Ballarat suburb of Sebastopol. Prosecutor Andrew Buckland told the court that while the group was at the house, an older sibling arrived with his friend, Young, to socialise in the shed. There, the larger group played pool, drank alcohol and sat by the fire. Hannah McGuire, 23, was murdered in her home in 2024 by her ex-partner, Lachlan Young. When some of the younger members of the group went to bed, Young had sat beside the complainant and asked for her Snapchat. Buckland said Young was then accused of asking if she “wanted to do something” but the girl refused and went to bed.



The pair allegedly continued to exchange messages, including the girl writing to Young: “do you know how old I am”, and “no, I’m 16″. The girl told the jury that about 3am, she agreed to meet Young in the backyard where she consented to him putting his hands into her shorts. He then allegedly asked, “Do you want to f---?” The girl told the court she said no, but accused Young of forcing himself onto her. The next day, the jury heard, the girl told one of her friends she was raped by Young. The trial heard that weeks later, she messaged Young to say, “how’s ya missus? How would she feel about f---ing an underage and cheating on her?” and later “you’re pathetic Lachie, you f---ed me even though I said no”.



Young blocked the girl, and she later reported the alleged rape to a school wellbeing counsellor who contacted police. Young (centre) is already serving a jail term of at least 22 years for murdering McGuire. Instagram During the trial, Young gave evidence and denied raping the teenage complainant. He told the jury that during the evening in February 2024 he had communicated “very little” with the girl over Snapchat, believing she was over 18. “She was there drinking alcohol and I overheard a conversation that they had been at the pub earlier that night,” he said.



Young said that about 6am the next day, he left the shed and the complainant came out to meet him. “One thing’s led to another and we’ve come on to each other. We started kissing,” Young told the court. The carpenter said that during this time, the girl told him she was 16 and he said he gently pushed her away. “I wasn’t interested in the age gap and I didn’t wanna go down that path of getting into trouble. I said, ‘Nothing more can happen’, and, ‘Sorry, but I’m not interested’,” Young told the jury. “Once I said that, I started to walk back to the shed and she’s sort of followed me and she said that it’s fine and no one will have to know and no one will get in any trouble. I said, ‘Sorry, I’m still not interested’, and I continued to walk back to the shed.”



Related Article Updated

Courts ‘I will never forgive,’ Hannah McGuire’s mother tells her daughter’s murderer Young maintained he and the girl were in the backyard together for about five minutes. He told the trial he later blocked her on Snapchat because he didn’t want to entertain claims he raped her. While under cross-examination, Young said: “I had a partner at home. I was doing the wrong thing and it shouldn’t have got to that stage and I pulled it up.” Young is already serving a jail term of 28 years, with a non-parole period of 22 years and four months, for what a judge last year described as the “brutal and callous” murder of McGuire, which was “extreme act of domestic violence”. Young strangled his ex-girlfriend on the bathroom floor of the home they once shared in Sebastopol, in Ballarat’s south, about 2.30am on April 5, 2024.

World.title: Nursing graduate applies for more than 100 jobs without success
World.content:
Nursing graduates who have applied for hundreds of jobs and have not found work say it's devastating to hear there's a shortage of nurses.

The nurse's union says Aotearoa's health system is falling into a deeper crisis, with emergency departments and wards bursting at the seams.

It follows revelations that Health New Zealand has hired just 54 full-time equivalent nurses in the past two years.

Nursing graduates struggle to find work while hospitals in crisis Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The situation is driving some graduates to consider making the move to Australia... joining their course mates who have already left.

After finishing hundreds of unpaid placement hours in Auckland, Megan completed her Bachelor of Nursing late last year.

In Aotearoa, new nurses have to apply for graduate positions, some do this through Te Whatu Ora's application system called ACE.

Others apply directly to private hospitals, community organisations and primary care.

But since graduating in March, Megan has applied for more than 100 nursing jobs and hasn't had any luck.

"I feel like I've failed, or there's something that I'm not showing in my application. I didn't realise it was going to be this hard to get a job."

Megan told Checkpoint she's getting by on the Jobseeker benefit while she continues to look for work.

If she can't find work soon, she's eyeing up Australia and said she may be forced to give up on nursing entirely.

"If I don't get a job I'm either likely going to have to re-study something else, or go into a completely different workforce.

"The running joke at the moment is that I become a flight attendant, which I don't really want to, but I've got to get a job somewhere."

Megan said it doesn't make sense how hard it is to find work because of reported shortages and staff burnout.

"We see constantly that the hospitals are understaffed and people are dying.

"Going into an election year, how can you promise us as nurses, new grads and even the public that the hospitals are going to be staffed?"

Hearing stories of graduates not being able to get work has students worried too.

Eden Sandhu is in her final year of studying nursing at Ara Institute of Canterbury.

But seeing nurses the year above missing out on jobs has made her anxious.

"Like thinking that there's no guarantee of securing a graduate position is just draining.

"We're told that there's a shortage, but all of us still experience anxiety that people aren't getting jobs, will there be a position for me when I graduate?"

To get their degrees, nurses have to complete hundreds of hours of on-the-job training, which is not paid.

Eden Sandhu said she had sacrificed so much financially to become qualified and worried about the future.

"[It's] a huge a worry because I've got a family and a mortgage... it's not okay to have graduates coming through having to consider after three years, to find something else."

Moving to Australia is something that's been on Eden's mind over the past few months.

"I think if New Zealand focused on supporting the students through placement, offering paid placements, upping the amount nurses are paid for the incredible stress levels they carry.

"Focussing on how to keep nurses here and not have such a terrible environment that people need to shoot off, that would change how I feel about leaving," she said.

"I would want to stay, I do want to stay, but unfortunately [if I don't find a job] I can't."

Dawn Blyth, the Nurses Organisation's National Student Unit co-leader, is also in her final year of study.

People in her cohort have already applied to Australia's graduate programmes.

"I graduate in November... we understand that jobs aren't guaranteed anywhere in any climate.

"But what is really hard to understand is how can we be saying that our country is so short of nurses... when there isn't the funds to put those nurses into jobs."

Health New Zealand national chief nurse Nadine Gray told Checkpoint they were offering a similar number of roles to last year to keep a mix of experienced and graduate nurses.

She said they were supporting all graduate registered nurses into employment, but this might not happen immediately, and they had never been able to employ every graduate nurse.

World.title: Woman and child seriously assaulted during Northland break in, man arrested
World.content:
A woman and her child were injured in an assaulted during an alleged break in at a Northland property.

Police have arrested a 38-year-old man following what they called a "violent aggravated robbery" in Kaikohe at 7am on Thursday.

Detective Senior Sergeant Aaron Crawford said police were called to a report of a man allegedly carrying a gun, breaking into a property on Williams St.

A woman and her child were inside, Crawford said, and the pair were "seriously assaulted" before a man fled in a car he stole from the home.

The police Eagle helicopter found the car a short time later in Ōmāpere.

Crawford said the man police believed was involved attempted to run and allegedly tried to steal another car by assaulting another person.

Police intervened, Crawford said, and took him into custody.

A gun and items police believed belonged to the home of the woman and child had since been found, he said.

The woman was taken to hospital in a serious but stable condition, Crawford said, and the child had minor injuries.

"Both are understandably shaken," he said.

The 38-year-old man was in custody and Crawford said charges were pending.

Police wanted to hear from anyone who saw what happened on Williams St or any sightings of a yellow Suzuki Swift travelling west on SH12 towards Whirinaki, Kouto Loop Rd and then Opononi and Ōmāpere.

They also wanted to hear from anyone who saw a man acting "suspiciously" in the Ōmāpere area on Thursday morning.

Information could be provided online at 105.police.govt.nz, or by calling 105 and using the reference number 260820/5258.

World.title: Mother of man murdered in Auckland Prison wants accountability from Corrections
World.content:
Mother of inmate stabbed to death wants corrections held accountable Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The mother of a man who was murdered in Auckland's maximum security prison wants the Corrections Department held accountable for his death.

Blake Lee was shanked to death by another inmate, in an exercise yard inside Auckland Prison at Paremoremo in March 2020.

A Coronial inquest into his death at the Auckland District Court heard details about Lee's transfer to the prison, just hours before he was murdered.

For Lee's mother, Teresa Absolum, it was the good things about her son she tried to remember.

"It's obviously very painful listening to the evidence as it brings feelings of sadness and anger at the way Blake died up," she said.

"I am trying to remember all the good things about my son."

Lee was killed in the prison yard, shortly after his transfer from Whanganui prison to Paremoremo.

The man responsible for his murder, Siuaki Lisiate, was a senior member of the Crips gang, while Lee was an affiliate of the Mongrel Mob.

In 2020, there was no set policy on where gang members should be placed in the prison.

Paremoremo's prison director at the time, David Pattinson, was asked if it was practical to separate rival gang members inside.

"Not unless we built a bigger jail," he said.

Photographs taken of Paremoremo's prison director at the time, David Pattinson, had to be blurred. Finn Blackwell / RNZ

"It would be difficult, there are principles around the style of people that comes together, what influence they can have on the rest of the prisoner group.

"We work hard to maintain a safer environment."

He was question by Susan Gray, the lawyer representing Lee's mother, about the risk of letting a newly transferred prisoner into the yard with different gang members.

"He enters into the yard, he greets people in the yard, they greet him," Pattinson said.

"He acts with confidence in that space, he looks comfortable in that environment, and unfortunately others intervene to change that for him."

Pattinson said at that point in time prior to the attack, it looked like a good decision to offer Lee the opportunity to exercise.

Two years prior, Lisiate had attacked double murderer Graeme Burton with a shank while both men were doing time in Paremoremo.

Gray asked Pattinson about Lisiate's violent past.

"You would agree, surely, that Mr Lisiate had a history of extreme violence," Gray asked.

"I don't disagree with that," Pattinson replied.

Lee's mother told RNZ she wanted to see members of rival gangs separated in prison.

"I would like Corrections to be accountable for my son's death but also for gang members from different gangs never to be mixed," she said.

But Pattinson told the lawyer representing Corrections, Claire Paterson, the murder was not gang related.

Blake Lee died at Auckland Prison in Paremoremo. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"A lot of work was done by Corrections in the aftermath of this tragic incident," Paterson said.

"Was there any evidence found that this was in fact a gang related incident," she asked.

There was no evidence to support that, Pattinson said.

That was despite an earlier High Court memorandum from Lisiate himself, describing gang tensions behind bars as ever-present.

Pattinson said if Lee was transferred to Paremoremo again today, he would likely be put in the same unit.

Later in the day, the inquest heard from the current prison director, Stephen Parr.

He said the protocols in place today would prevent Lee from being placed into a mix on the day of his arrival.

Parr spoke about the shank Lisiate had, saying it was not uncommon for makeshift weapons to be made from items in the prison environment.

"The screening procedures in place were then and are now considered appropriate, however, no procedure is foolproof nor immune to human error," he said.

"It is unfortunate that these procedures were not completed to the required or expected standard on that day."

Parr said he was not in a position to definitively say whether correct scanning procedures would have detected Lisiate's shank.

"Staff acted in accordance with the process that was in place at the time in placing Mr Lee in the yard with that mix of gangs," he said.

World.title: NZ Cricket boss Geoff Allott says $7.3 million deficit forecast 'not good enough'
World.content:
New Zealand Cricket has announced a preliminary deficit of $7.3 million for the last financial year and is planning on slashing the broadcast schedule for the final T20 Super Smash season as part of cost-cutting measures.

The preliminary deficit announced on Thursday by NZ Cricket (NZC) is significantly higher than the budget forecast deficit of $1.8m for the financial year ending 31 July 2026.

In a media release, New Zealand Cricket (NZC) primarily attributes the difference to the organisation budgeting for revenue from a multi-year domestic broadcast contract, which had already been received in previous financial years.

It said a reduction in income following changes to NZC's partnership with sponsor Dream11, prompted by changes to India's gambling laws, together with an increase in the organisation's overall costs, also contributed to the deficit.

NZC chief executive Geoff Allott acknowledged the situation was disappointing, but believed the game was still in good financial health.

"As an organisation we accept that this financial performance isn't good enough, nor is it sustainable," he said.
